Overarching argument: Paul treats machine learning and NLP applied to public political text (congressional floor speech, public statements, lobbying filings) as a way to produce actor-level attributes (personality traits, policy positions, emotion) that can be placed on nodes of a social-network-analysis graph. The purpose he names is political intelligence: lobbying strategy, industry alignment, and how to pitch policy to a specific member of Congress.

Research questions and gaps Paul states:
1. Conversion step. Birkenmaier and Lechner, Peng et al., and Ramey et al. each say the pipeline does not specify how a model's output becomes a graph node or vector. This is the most repeated gap in the document.
2. Ambiguity. Birkenmaier and Lechner say the method does not separate ambiguous statements.
3. Conflict. Kim et al. do not show inter-industry conflict over a specific bill, which Paul says matters for political intelligence.
4. Temporal lag. Kim et al. are reactive, not predictive, because filing reports lag current positions.
5. Model limits. Peng et al. say long-distance dependency is the main obstacle for most emotion models; stacking reduces but does not remove it.
6. Venue coverage. Ramey et al. offer no pipeline for textual venues beyond their own, and Paul says a framework for contextual or auditory constraints is also needed.

Synthesis: Birkenmaier and Lechner and Ramey et al. both concern personality measurement from speech or text, with Ramey et al. as the older foundation and Birkenmaier and Lechner as the newer, codebook-backed method. Kim et al. and Birkenmaier and Lechner both concern the actor-to-graph link. Peng et al. supplies the model landscape that the other two would run on.

Self-declared gap: Paul says his own technical grounding is not yet sufficient for Peng et al. and plans a second reading after more background.

works.title: Twitter as Data
works.summary:
**What the paper is.** This is a short Cambridge Elements methods tutorial on collecting and processing Twitter data for social scientists. The excerpt on disk covers printed pages 1-10 only and stops partway through section 2.1.1. There is no estimator, no test and no causal design. Its content is descriptive figures from 2016 and a description of the data pipes:
- **Scale:** 319M monthly active users and about 500M tweets a day.
- **US adult usage:** 24% use Twitter; 42% of users use it daily.
- **Elite coverage:** every Senator and 430 House members have official accounts.
- **Geotags:** geotagged tweets are about 2-3% of traffic and skew urban and higher-income.
- **Access limits:** the streaming API gives about a 1% sample with no information on the author's network. The REST API caps each account at its 3,200 most recent tweets and is needed to rebuild follower networks. Author metadata reflects the time of the API request, not the time the tweet was posted.

The rest of the excerpt compares R packages (streamR, twitteR, RCurl) with Python packages (twython, tweepy, pandas). Network analysis is deferred to a separate 2016 work by the same author.

**Why it matters here, and how little.** The system's social channel does not use the Twitter API at all. X, Facebook and Truth Social posts come from a licensed Quorum export; Bluesky posts are collected directly. The social network layer is built from reposts and @mentions found in post text, not from follower or friend lists. So the 3,200-tweet cap, the rate limits and the stream-sampling limits do not bind on the system as built.

Two points do carry over, both as context:
- **Coverage:** the elite-coverage figure supports the assumption that nearly every member has a social channel to read, though the figure is from 2016.
- **Metadata timing:** handle-to-member mapping and attribution happen at collection time. This is a provenance caveat for the member-attributed corpus.

Nothing in the excerpt bears on stance classification, influence modeling, path-finding or allocation. Its access claims describe the 2016 API and the 2016 platform, not today's X.
works.question: No testable research question. The Element aims to introduce social scientists to acquiring, processing and analyzing Twitter data, with scripts and examples (p.1).
works.method:
Methods tutorial. Covers acquisition via the REST API (user timelines, specific tweet IDs, search, follower and friend lists) and the streaming API (random 1 percent sample, filters by language, keyword, account, place) (pp.2, 5, 10). Then processing raw tweets into rectangular data, text analysis, event detection, spatial analysis of geotagged tweets (pp.2-3, 7). Software: R (streamR, twitteR, RCurl) and Python (twython, tweepy, pandas, statsmodels, NLP and ML libraries) (pp.7-9). No estimator, model or statistical test appears in the excerpt.</method>
<parameter name="identification">Not applicable. No causal or identification strategy in the excerpt.

works.title: Image as Data: Automated Content Analysis for Visual Presentations of Political Actors and Events
works.summary:
Joo and Steinert-Threlkeld (CCR 2022) is a methods tutorial on treating images as data, with two applications. Study 1 sends 15,647 Facebook photos from 677 candidates in 2018 through Google's label API. It runs chi-squared tests of label against party separately by gender, because the parties' gender ratios differ. Republican men over-index labels like Official and Military officer. Republican women over-index Blond and Red. There is no correction for testing about 1,700 labels. Study 2 fine-tunes a ResNet-50 (91.79% accuracy) on protest images from five protest episodes. It defines framing as the share of near-duplicate images per event and frame label, where a duplicate is a normalized feature distance below 0.2, a threshold picked from one histogram. H1 (state violence shared more than protester violence) and H2 (crowds shared more than individuals) each hold in 3 of 5 events. The authors call the results provisional. There is no causal identification.

For Paul's systems, the paper matters in one place. fec/network/frame_alignment.py ports both instruments to text: near-duplicate press titles across members (3-word-shingle Jaccard >= 0.5), and chi-squared category and term association with party. Checking the code showed that the transfer breaks on the unit of analysis. Joo's sharer chooses the image. The text port reads cu_press_stance_tone.csv with no source filter, and 816 of its 2,388 rows are americascreditunions.org articles that are attributed to each member they mention. One ACU headline credited to many members therefore counts as members echoing one script. In a single-path recompute that is UNVERIFIED under DE-062, General CU duplication falls from 60.2% (n=442) to 5.2% (n=116), and CU Tax Status from 64.7% (n=190) to 38.1% (n=42), once only *.senate.gov and *.house.gov rows are kept. The output is a diagnostic, last written 2026-07-01. It reaches salience_shock only under `--intensity auto`, and the chain does not pass that flag.
works.question: Can large-scale image data be analyzed with deep learning / convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to measure political communication that text methods and small manual codings cannot reach? Two applied questions: (1) how U.S. politicians' Facebook photographs differ by party and gender, measured with an off-the-shelf label API; (2) how protest images shared on Twitter frame events, with testable expectations that protest images emphasize state violence over protester violence (H1) and crowds over individuals (H2).
works.method: Study 1: off-the-shelf Google Vision Label Detection (no training); label prevalence by party computed as the share of images with each label (pD, pR); chi-squared test per label, separate for male and female candidates; labels sorted by chi-square (Tables 1-2, printed p.28-29). Unsupervised check: ImageNet-pretrained CNN features (2,048-dim penultimate layer), k-means with k=200 (Appendix F, printed p.54-55). Study 2: fine-tuned ResNet-50 (He et al. 2016) for protest image classification and for violence/police/fire/sign labels; FairFace classifier (Karkkainen and Joo 2019) for face sex, race and age; six frame labels (contains child, faces, large group, small group, protester violence, state violence); duplicate detection via cosine-style pairwise distance on the 1,000-dim last fully connected layer, duplicate if normalized distance below 0.2 (threshold chosen by inspecting the histogram); framing rate = share of duplicate images within each event-label (Table 3, printed p.33). Background sections describe CNN architecture, transfer learning, training, validation (Grad-CAM visualization, Appendix D) and ethics. Table D1 compares architectures (AlexNet, VGG-16/19, ResNet-18/34/50) for protest fine-tuning.

works.title: Big data-assisted social media analytics for business model for business decision making system competitive analysis
works.summary:
Zhang et al. (2022) propose BD-SMAB, a conceptual decision-support framework for business competitive analysis built from social media. It chains together several standard pieces: DMN decision modelling; Affin-lexicon and ensemble-classifier labelling of praise versus complaint; NMF clustering; an L1-penalised linear model of market-value change on phrase-intensity change (Eqs. 1-2); z-scored one-day burst detection over trailing 5- and 25-day windows (|z|>30); a term co-occurrence graph (cross-correlation >= 0.1) partitioned with Louvain; and a hotness index He(t), the sum of sentiment times volume over bursting events. The case study covers 882,371 tweets about five retailers, collected by VOZIQ, a commercial partner one author worked with. Its outputs are descriptive only: Costco category positive shares (jewelry 91%, parking 39%) and mention shares (Wal-Mart 35%, Costco 24%; window and denominator not stated). The paper has no holdout, no baseline and no metrics. Its "highest accuracy" claim has no numbers behind it. The authors call the framework conceptual. The company list is inconsistent, the equations are garbled, and several citations are wrong (the Affin citation points to a photonics paper).

For Paul's systems this is a weak, context-level source. The closest overlaps are methodological. Louvain on a thresholded correlation graph is what press_hcoi.py already does, using Malaterre's 0.6 threshold. A volume-and-sentiment burst index is a possible time-varying trigger for the salience-shock engine, whose uncertainty and polarization terms are currently static and estimated from the stance matrix. The paper does not validate any of these components, so nothing in it can justify changing a threshold, half-life or weight. Any idea taken from it starts out UNVERIFIED.
works.question: Stated objective (Sec. 1, p. 3 of the text, "Introduction"): "the objective of this study is to check the usefulness of the development and implementation of an integrative management information system." The abstract frames it as whether a Big Data-assisted social media analytics model (BD-SMAB) can help decision-makers with marketing strategy and competitive analysis. No explicit hypotheses or formal research questions are stated.
works.method: Conceptual framework plus a descriptive case study. Components: (1) DMN-style decision modeling in two layers, decision requirements diagrams and decision logic (Sec. 2 and 3); (2) sentiment and phrase classification: Affin lexicon phrase scores, ensemble machine-learning classifiers on hybrid features to label praise vs complaint, and nonnegative matrix factorization for clustering (Sec. 1, around lines 125 and 129); (3) a linear model relating market value changes to weighted phrase/search-intensity changes, ΔC(t+1)=Σ w_k Δx_k(t) (Eq. 1), with weights estimated under an L1 penalty λΣ|w_k| (Eq. 2; the text writes "argmax" but a penalized least-squares minimization is described); (4) z-score normalization of 1-day variations over trailing n-day windows (Eq. 3; n=5 and 25 mentioned, burst threshold |z|>30); (5) burst detection on term frequency, a term co-occurrence/cross-correlation graph (threshold 0.1), Louvain community detection, and an event hotness index He(t)=Σ sentiment×volume over bursting events (Eq. 5); (6) Leximancer concept mapping and VOZIQ category/sentiment dashboards for the case study (Sec. 3.1). Eq. (1) and Eq. (2) are garbled in the extraction, so exact notation should be checked against the PDF.

works.title: Evaluating voice samples as a potential source of information about personality
works.summary:
Marrero, Gosling, Pennebaker and Harari (2022) took one short smartphone voice sample (mean 92 words, about 51 s) from each of 614 UT Austin intro-psychology students. They used XGBoost with Tree-SHAP feature selection to predict self-reported BFI-2 traits from 94 LIWC-2015 dimensions and 272 pyAudioAnalysis vocal features. The fit metric is out-of-sample R-squared from 100-fold CV, and the paper gives no permutation null. Averaged across the Big Five, the joint feature set explained 10.67% of variance, vocal features alone 6.24% and LIWC alone 3.13%. Extraversion, Conscientiousness and Neuroticism reached 10-20% with the joint set, Openness stayed under 10%, and gender was predicted at over 90%. The authors say the joint result is more than the sum of the two parts, but they give no causal identification and the criterion is self-report.

This paper is not new to the system. It was the stated method source for `big5_audio_faithful_prereg.md` and was cited in Addendum 1 of `big5_audio_prereg.md`. In July 2026 Melange ran three one-look audio tests at N=90 legislators. Two findings partly carried over: a full eGeMAPS-88 ridge predicted Pink-E (held-out r +0.284, perm-p .030) and Pink-ES (r +0.298, perm-p .017). The paper's headline did not carry over. Super-additivity missed every time: vocal added +0.001 over linguistic for E against Pink, and -0.004 over text against behavioural visibility. Voice did not measure C (r -0.081). The A-ES halo got worse (|r| 0.819 and 0.946).

What the paper means for the system as built: it is the benchmark the audio lane has already tested and largely failed to reproduce in legislators. It explains why audio is display-only, and it does not support moving audio into the engine. Two leads remain open. Its top features (MFCC, chroma, spectral entropy, deltas) are mostly missing from eGeMAPS-88. It also shows reliability disattenuation, which the system never applies to its validity coefficients.
works.question: (1) How much information about personality (Big Five, self-report) is conveyed by the linguistic (LIWC 2015) and vocal (pyAudioAnalysis) features of short, semi-structured voice samples? (2) Do semi-structured voice samples reveal more about some personality traits than others? Secondary benchmarks: depression, age and gender (p.2, lines 148-156; p.4).
works.method: Two-stage, automated machine learning pipeline in R 4.1.2 (mlr 2.19.0, mlrMBO 1.1.5) with XGBoost (1.5.2.1) as the learner (p.3-4). Stage 1 (global search): 150 Latin Hypercube hyperparameter configurations, each scored by 10-fold CV; a Gaussian Process surrogate and CMA-ES then propose new configurations for sequential model-based optimization, run for at least 50 cycles (extended while improvement continued) (p.4). Feature set fixed at 100%. Stage 2 (feature selection): nested 10-fold CV within each outer fold, Tree SHAP values for each test sample, a pseudo partial R-squared per feature (R-squared of model with the feature's SHAP removed vs. full model), repeated five times and weighted by error; top-30 features kept per outer fold and XGBoost refit with stage-1 hyperparameters held fixed; performance is the mean over the 10 outer folds (p.4). Evaluation: out-of-sample R-squared for regression defined as 1 minus CV test MSE divided by outcome variance (p.4). For classification, log loss is used rather than AUC, and scored as 1 minus model log loss over intercept-only log loss (p.5). Uncertainty: no standard test fits the repeated selection, so final models were re-estimated with 100-fold CV (about 9% more training data per fold), on the assumption that a generalizable model improves with more data (p.5). Post-hoc: reliability (Cronbach alpha, mean feature test-retest correlation) used to disattenuate performance (Spearman 1961) and to test whether scale reliability predicts model performance (p.7-8).

works.title: Large Language Model Enhanced Logic Tensor Network for Stance Detection
works.summary:
Dai et al. (Neural Networks 183, 2025) propose FOLAR, a stance detector with three parts. First, chain-of-thought prompts ask an LLM to write a first-order-logic (FOL) rule for each text and target. Second, a logic tensor network (LTN) uses a shared BERT and soft operators (negation 1-U, product conjunction, implication 1-U1+U1U2) to turn the rule into a differentiable classifier. Third, the LTNs built from GPT-3.5, Claude-2 and LLaMA-2 are fused by attention routing. The tests use English political tweets (SemEval-2016, ISD) and VAST. On in-target SEM16 and ISD the gains are small: +1.7 F_avg on LA and +2.0 on DT_I, and FOLAR is not the best on FM or HC. Zero-shot VAST gains are larger: +4.2 with full training data and +6.2 with 10% of it. The fusion ablation is about 5.8 points, but it compares fusion with a single GPT-3.5 model, so fusion is not separated from the choice of LLM. The paper reports no standard deviations, does not name its significance test, and its tables contain internal inconsistencies. The interpretability claim rests only on a 100-item, 3-rater check.

For Paul's system, the paper matters most as a formal version of something already built. The two-hop CU-alignment rule in fec/stance/apply_two_hop_stance.py composes stance with valence by hard sign multiplication over a hand-curated registry. FOLAR is the soft, learned, LLM-elicited form of that rule. It also gives a candidate route for the registry-coverage problem, but its error analysis (the LLM linking unrelated positive words to the target) names the same failure that sank the system's automatic-registry variants. The fusion result points to a cheap check on single-labeller bias in the Claude pre-labels that the DEBATE reader distils. It does not show that switching to FOLAR would beat a fine-tuned DEBATE or SVM on 87 to 156 held-out CU press items. The domain, the text genre and the LLM versions all differ.
works.question: Can first-order logic (FOL) rules elicited from LLMs by chain-of-thought prompting be encoded in a logic tensor network (LTN), and can fusing LTNs built from several LLMs produce interpretable and more accurate stance detection than fine-tuned PLMs, prompt-tuning, and LLM-only baselines, in both in-target and zero-shot settings?
works.method: FOLAR = three modules. (a) Knowledge Elicitation (Sec 3.1): chain-of-thought prompts ask an LLM to produce a FOL rule for each input and target, illustrated by Eq 1 and Table 5. (b) LTN (Sec 3.2): predicates are phrases embedded by a shared pretrained BERT, followed by fully connected layers; soft-logic operators are negation 1-U, conjunction product, disjunction U1+U2-U1U2, implication 1-U1+U1U2 (Eqs 2-5); output is a softmax over favor/neutral/against (Eq 6 composition). (c) Multi-Decision Fusion (Sec 3.3): one LTN per LLM (GPT-3.5, LLaMA-2, Claude-2), representation vectors concatenated into H and fused by attention-based dynamic routing over t iterations with layer normalization and sigmoid (Eqs 7-11); training minimizes cross-entropy (Eq 12). Training: AdamW, batch 16, up to 30 epochs, warm-up ratio 0.2, learning rate 1e-5, weight decay 1e-3. Baselines (Sec 4.4): statistical (Bicond, CrossNet, SEKT, TPDG); PLM (JoinCL, PT-HCL, TarBK, SDAgu, KPT, KEprompt, BERT-FT); LLM (Ts-CoT, KASD, MPPT, COLA) plus FOL-CoT (the LLM-only variant of FOLAR). Ablations: w/o FOL (compared to Ts-CoT-like structure), w/o LTN, w/o MDF (single GPT-3.5).

works.title: Going Global: 39 Language Versions of the BFI-2-XS
works.summary: Rammstedt and colleagues document how the 15-item BFI-2-XS (and the 30-item BFI-2-S where fielded) was translated into 39 versions for 29 countries in 24 languages for the PIAAC 2023 social-emotional skills module. The procedure is a modified TRAPD: reuse and review of pre-existing translations for 15 languages, double translation plus reconciliation for nine languages (12 versions), national and expert review, independent linguistic verification, and Field Trial pretesting on nearly 30,000 respondents. Change requests were coded into a customized MQM error typology. Before the Field Trial, gendering drove 49 percent of requests and, on average, 10 percent of BFI-2-S items changed per version (range 0 to 80 percent). After it, 13 of 39 versions changed, averaging 6 percent of XS items. The paper is instrument documentation. It reports no reliability, factor structure or invariance results, because Field Trial data are confidential, and the authors say the versions are not yet fully validated. Their comparability claim rests on the procedure, not on data. For Paul's systems the bearing is thin. Melange reads Big Five traits from English political text with closed-vocabulary rates and a 20-item IPIP-style LLM rater, not with self-report questionnaires, and it does no translation. Two transferable lessons follow. First, small wording changes are treated as material to comparability, which matches the itemset versioning the LLM reader already does. Second, comparability across administrations is asserted procedurally rather than shown, which is the gap the system itself hit when interview-derived affective N failed to transfer to floor and hearing text. The paper offers no validity evidence that the system could borrow.

works.title: The Kernel of Truth in Text-Based Personality Assessment: A Meta-Analysis of the Relations Between the Big Five and the Linguistic Inquiry and Word Count (LIWC)
works.summary:
Koutsoumpis et al. (Psychological Bulletin, 2022; the vault slug says 2024, the PDF says 2022) pooled 31 samples (N = 85,724). They correlated Big Five scores with the 52 LIWC categories shared by LIWC2001, 2007 and 2015.

**Self-reports (cue validity), 26 samples.** Effects are small. The strongest correlations run |rho| .08-.14, and all 52 categories together explain about 5.1% of trait variance.

**Observer ratings (cue utilization), only 5 samples (n = 1,637).** Effects are larger: |rho| .18-.39, with R2 averaging 38.5%.

**Overlap.** Only 20 of 260 trait-by-category markers agree in direction for both self and observer reports. The paper calls this the "kernel of truth". Examples: swear words, anger and negative emotion for low Conscientiousness and low Agreeableness, and negative emotion for low Emotional Stability.

**Other results.** Heterogeneity is nearly universal: 96% of self-report effects and 82% of observer effects. Formal settings weaken some markers, for example Agreeableness with swear words is -.07 formal vs -.14 informal. Spoken text carries much more Extraversion signal through word count than written text (.23 vs .03). LIWC also trails other computer methods (.10 vs .27-.31).

**Why it matters for Melange.** The system's lexical Big Five (`big5_traits.py`) is this closed-vocabulary method applied to formal congressional speech. It uses short published-exemplar word lists, not licensed LIWC dictionaries. The paper sets a low ceiling on how much true trait signal such rates can carry. That supports four existing choices: the brain's reading that the RKH convergence (CV mean .350) is inflated by shared method, retiring the lexical basis from the receptivity layer, square-root token shrinkage, and keeping status labels on any external claim.

The paper also gives a direction check for the active SMOreg weights, and some of them point the opposite way. Finally, observer-panel passes need care. The paper says plainly that valid cues are not the same as true personality, so convergence with the Senate expert panels may partly reflect raters using the same cues the text model uses (utilization), not validity.
works.question: Do self-reported and observer-reported Big Five traits correlate with the 52 LIWC categories shared across LIWC2001, LIWC2007 and LIWC2015 (cue validity and cue utilization)? Which categories form a "kernel of truth" that both self- and observer-reports link to? Do 10 study, sample and task moderators explain heterogeneity in these effects? (Introduction, pp. 843-847.)
works.method: PRISMA-reported systematic review followed by meta-analysis (random-effects model, R package "meta"). Effect size: Pearson r, Fisher z transformation and back-transformation; Spearman rho converted to r for one study. Corrected effects (rho) disattenuated for personality-measure reliability only (Cronbach alpha for self-reports; ICC for observer reports); LIWC categories not corrected. Missing effect sizes (12% of values) imputed with a self-devised "mean minus 1" rule (sum of available effects plus zeros, divided by k-1); analyses based on this rule (pp. 847-849). Heterogeneity: Cochran Q, I2, tau. Publication bias: Egger's test on uncorrected, nonimputed data. Moderators (five categorical: LIWC version, written-spoken, formality, synchronicity, sample composition; five continuous: sample size, text length, age, percentage women, publication year) tested with meta-regression. Explained variance per trait: meta-analytic linear regression of each trait on all LIWC categories in lavaan, using a 52-category weighted average correlation matrix from 14 studies (n = 6,405) and the harmonic mean n. Content vs function words analysed separately, using narrow categories only to avoid double counting. Two coders per study (first author coded all; four research assistants coded a quarter each).

works.title: Twenty Years of Personality Computing: Threats, Challenges and Future Directions
works.summary:
Celli and colleagues review about twenty years of Personality Computing. They follow PRISMA 2020 and report 129 included papers, although the screening arithmetic in the paper gives 126. The review covers three tasks: Recognition (self-reported traits), Perception (traits as observers judge them) and Synthesis (traits that machines generate). Across text, image, audio, video, hybrid and LLM systems, the reported state of the art is modest. Text recognition reaches an average correlation of about 0.30 against a 0.133 baseline. Zero-shot GPT models reach r = 0.29 on Facebook posts, about the same as specialized models. Computer perception has a convergent validity of 0.30, against 0.38 for human judges, and the authors warn that these settings are not fully comparable. Most text systems are SVMs on psycholinguistic features (LIWC/MRC), drawn from Essays and social-network data. Biel et al. found that Extraversion carries the most audio-visual cues and Emotional Stability the fewest. The review recommends reporting rank correlations rather than median splits, judges MBTI and DISC invalid, and calls LLM personality a safety problem. It also lists personality-aware persuasion in elections as a threat.

For Melange, the paper sets an outside ceiling on what text- and audio-derived traits can deliver. It also places the system's validation targets on Brunswik's lens model. The RKH comparison is Recognition against a target that uses the same method as the system. The Personality on the Hill panels are Perception. Neither is a self-report criterion, so the system's figures do not line up with the paper's state-of-the-art rows. The paper also explains why the system was right to move receptivity off lexical traits and onto behavior. The cue pattern by modality suggests that audio work should start with Extraversion, not Neuroticism. Every cross-study comparison below is UNVERIFIED (DE-062); no second path has reproduced it.

works.method: Narrative/systematic review following PRISMA 2020 (p.12). Search combined modality keywords with personality aliases on the web and in Google Scholar and Scopus. Iterative reference-list expansion to transitive closure. Scopus citation network built in Gephi, with in-degree of 5 or more shown as a foundational-works graph (Fig. 2, p.6-7). Two-phase screening: inclusive first pass, then a pruning pass that excluded inconsistent or flawed work (small samples, weak train/validation/test setup, no comparison to prior methods, unavailable data or code; example Souri et al. [252] excluded, p.12). A single reviewer handled valid articles; at least one more reviewer handled exclusion candidates (p.12). Separate state-of-the-art (SotA) table limited to open-science works, Big Five targets, and F1, accuracy or Rho metrics (Table 3, p.10-11). Section 3 categorizes systems by data modality with Big Five cue tables (Tables 5, 9, 11) and algorithm/feature/data-source matrices (Tables 4, 6, 7, 8, 10, 12). Section 3.5 surveys 10 LLM-ethics papers (Table 13).

works.title: Predicting the Big 5 personality traits from digital footprints on social media: A meta-analysis
works.summary:
Azucar, Marengo and Settanni (Personality and Individual Differences 124, 2018; online December 2017) pooled 16 independent studies from 14 papers. They ran one random-effects meta-analysis per trait on untransformed Pearson r. The criterion in every study was a self-report Big Five inventory (BFI, TIPI or IPIP) from ordinary users of Facebook, Twitter, Sina Weibo or Instagram, with literature searched up to May 2017. The pooled correlations were: Openness .39, Conscientiousness .35, Extraversion .40, Agreeableness .29 (the lowest) and Neuroticism .33. The authors found no publication bias. Heterogeneity was very large (I² ≥ 93.15, every Q(15) significant). In univariate meta-regressions, using several types of footprint raised accuracy for O, C and N. Adding demographics raised it for A and N. Activity statistics (friends, posts, network density) raised it for E only marginally (β .19, p .06). Text and pictures alone added nothing. The pooled numbers are optimistic, because each study contributed its best model or strongest feature.

For Paul's systems this is a calibration paper, not a validation of them. Melange scores members of Congress, whose posts and press output are written by staff, against RKH estimates, which are themselves derived from text, and against Senate expert and insider panels. Neither of those is self-report from the members. The lexical reader's held-out CV against RKH has a mean of .350. That sits inside Azucar's range by coincidence of scale, not by comparable design, so it should never be presented as matching the meta-analytic benchmark. The paper offers three sharper lessons:
- Agreeableness is the least recoverable trait from digital footprints, which supports the system's move from lexical A to behavioural cooperation.
- Activity counts are at best a marginal Extraversion signal.
- Demographics improve "accuracy" only because group membership correlates with self-reported traits. The system's affective-N gate removes exactly that signal on purpose.

These pooled figures cover 16 studies of lay users and are UNSTRATIFIED across platforms. The authors could not test differences between platforms.
works.question: Estimate the mean predictive validity (Pearson r) of social-media digital footprints for each Big 5 trait; test whether the types of footprint used, the platform's default privacy setting (public vs. private), and study quality moderate prediction accuracy; check for publication bias; and assess whether accuracy is consistent across traits (Abstract; Sec. 1.3, p.151).
works.method:
Five separate random-effects meta-analyses, one per Big 5 trait, using untransformed Pearson r (Fisher z explicitly rejected, citing Schmidt & Hunter, 2014; Sec. 2.4, p.153). Conversions: R^2 to r by square root (n=2); AUROC to Cohen's d to r (n=1); sensitivity/specificity or PPV/NPV to odds ratio to d to r (n=1); non-r reports converted (n=4). Where a study had several models or features, the best model or highest feature effect was used (Sec. 2.4, p.152-153). Outliers: Grubbs test (none found). Heterogeneity: Q, tau^2, I^2. Publication bias: funnel plot, Begg-Mazumdar and Egger tests, trim-and-fill, classic fail-safe N. Moderators: univariate random-effects meta-regression, REML, alpha 0.05, p<0.10 discussed; a moderator was tested only if at least 4 studies per group (Fu et al., 2014). Quality groups were pooled as low+medium (2+2) vs high (12) to reach the minimum. Software: Comprehensive Meta-analysis v3.3.070 (Sec. 2.4, p.153-154; Sec. 3.2.3, p.154).</method>

works.title: Comparing Fine-Tuned RoBERTa with Traditional Machine Learning Models for Stance Detection in Political Tweets
works.summary:
Khan et al. (2025) built a Roman Urdu dataset of Pakistani political tweet-and-reply pairs, about 8,374 labelled agree, disagree or unrelated. They benchmarked five TF-IDF classifiers against a fine-tuned RoBERTa. Reported accuracy: random forest 0.95, SVM 0.94, logistic regression 0.93, decision tree 0.92, naive bayes 0.89, all on 1,675 test rows. RoBERTa reached 0.97, but on an "augmented" set with support 6,699, so it was not scored on the same test split as the others. There is one 80/20 split, with no kappa, no seeds, no hyperparameters and no confidence intervals. The augmentation is described with image operations (rotation, flipping), and the conclusion contradicts the results section. As evidence the paper is weak. The ranking gaps of 1 to 4 points have no error bars, and the transformer-wins headline is not a like-for-like comparison.

It still matters here because the system cites it as a method source. fec/stance/train_stance_domain.py is literally titled "Khan et al. pipeline". It copies the paired target-conditioned input, the five-classifier ladder, the class-balancing analog and the expectation that "transformer should beat all". fec/stance/stance_eval.py takes macro-F1 as its headline and adds "unrelated" as a class "per ICCK/TACS" practice. On Paul's own data the paper's two transferable claims did not hold. A transformer on the augmented press set scored 0.757 macro-F1, below a tuned word+char LinearSVC at 0.816. The Khan multi-view augmentation hurt the classical models and was rejected on 2026-07-03. The lasting value is in the evaluation conventions: "unrelated" as its own class, macro-F1 as the headline, and fine-tuning only once labels are clean. The model-ranking claims do not carry over. The code docstring repeats the paper's 0.93 to 0.97 figures as if they were faithful, comparable numbers. It should flag that RoBERTa was scored on a different test set.
works.question: Can a fine-tuned RoBERTa model, and five traditional machine learning classifiers on TF-IDF features, classify stance (agree / disagree / unrelated) in Roman Urdu political tweets and replies, and which performs best? A secondary aim is to release a labeled Roman Urdu political stance dataset, since none was publicly available (Abstract p.78; Intro objectives p.80).
works.method: Preprocessing: stop-word removal, tokenization, POS tagging, lowercasing, lemmatization and phonetic spelling normalization (Section 3.3, pp.86-87). Features: TF-IDF for the classical models (pp.88-91). Classifiers: logistic regression (Eq. 5), decision tree with entropy/information gain (Eqs. 6-7), SVM with margin objective and kernel (Eqs. 8-10; kernel type not stated), random forest with majority vote (Eqs. 11-13; number of trees not stated), naive bayes (Eqs. 14-15). Deep model: RoBERTa fine-tuned on the concatenated tweet and comment, with a [CLS] classification head and softmax (pp.91-92). Dataset augmentation and class balancing are said to be applied (p.91), but the augmentation is described with image operations (rotation, flipping, color changes) and no text-augmentation procedure is given. Platform: Google Colab, Python (Section 4.1, p.88). Metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, F1 (Section 3.6, p.87). No hyperparameters, epochs, seeds, cross-validation, confidence intervals or significance tests are reported.

works.title: Artificial Intelligence and Sentiment Analysis: A Review in Competitive Research
works.summary:
Taherdoost and Madanchian (2023) is a scoping review, not an empirical study. They searched Scopus for 2012-2022 journal papers that combine AI or machine learning with sentiment analysis and business or competitive terms. Of 133 hits, 43 papers were kept; the text also says 90 were examined and never reconciles the two counts. The review counts papers by year, subject, keyword, author country and citations. Its narrative section repeats claims from the papers it cites. The one useful methodological point is borrowed from Alantari et al. (2022): neural-network classifiers predict best but diagnose poorly, and topic models do the reverse. The review runs no accuracy tests of its own. It does not separate sentiment from stance or address target-dependent valence. It does not cover political text, and it describes no quality appraisal or dual screening.

For the system as built, its bearing is thin. The CU stance stack already does what the review recommends, in a stricter form. stage5_debate.py uses a fine-tuned transformer NLI reader for direction, validated on held-out human gold: 0.839, kappa 0.742, n=87, member-grouped. Lexicoder LSD2015 is kept only as a tone-intensity term (stage5_lsd.R; run_stage5.R:141-143) and never decides direction. The predictive-versus-diagnostic split gives a framing for that division: the neural reader handles prediction and the transparent dictionary handles interpretable intensity. But that rests on consumer-review evidence and one cited study. The review says nothing about the system's real bottleneck, the valence hop at 0.689 in the two-hop decomposition, or about adversarial and sign-flip targets (0.571 on goldeval). Treat it as background, not as evidence for any component's design or constants.
works.question: RQ1: What is the current state of research on AI-based sentiment analysis in competitive research (document type, subject area, keywords, author geography, most-cited work)? RQ2: What is the development of the major AI-based sentiment analysis approaches? RQ3: What are the difficulties and prospects of AI-based sentiment analysis in competitive research? (Section 3.1, p.4.) Stated aim: help new researchers keep up with the field and improve future research quality (p.2).
works.method: Scoping review following a PRISMA-style flow (Figure 1, image only). Boolean search strings combining AI / artificial intelligence / machine learning / deep learning with "Sentiment Analysis" and business terms (Competitive, Business, Market, Customer, Product, Service) (Table 1, pp.5-6). Descriptive bibliometric tallies (year, document type, subject area, keywords, author country, citation counts) and narrative review of selected papers for RQ2-RQ3. No quality appraisal, dual coding or inter-rater procedure is described; author contributions list H.T. for methodology and validation (p.13).

works.title: How to train your stochastic parrot: large language models for political texts
works.summary:
Ornstein, Blasingame and Truscott (PSRM 2025, DOI 10.1017/psrm.2024.64) test few-shot prompts to GPT-3 and GPT-4 on four political text tasks. The tasks are sentiment in 945 SCOTUS tweets, tone in 935 campaign ads, ideology in 18,263 sentences from UK manifestos, and virtue-topic labels for 9,565 House one-minute speeches. On the tweets, GPT-3 got 88.4% of negative/positive signs right, against 64.3% for TweetNLP, 57.7% for Naive Bayes and 38.3% for the best dictionary. On ideology, LLM scores correlate with expert scores at rho 0.92 (economic) and 0.80 (social) across the 18 manifestos. LLM topic labels beat three random intruders in 80% of 400 blinded checks, where chance is 25%. Costs dropped about 1000-fold compared with crowd coding.

Three method points matter more than the headline numbers:
- Continuous measures are built from the label probability vector, not the argmax label.
- GPT-4, tuned with human feedback (RLHF), is overconfident. For over 70% of posts it put more than 99% on one label, and it chose Neutral more often than the human coders.
- Validation runs in three steps: tune the prompt on one hand-labelled set, check it on a second, then apply.

The authors also warn that the GPT-3 models they used were retired in January 2024, so the results cannot be reproduced.

For Paul's system, the paper does not bear on networks, money or allocation. It bears on the stance and text layer. Melange already supplies outside context in the prompt for its Claude stance rater, and it caches LLM outputs by model. The gaps are elsewhere:
- run_stage5.R throws away DEBATE's per-label probabilities and keeps only a sign, which is then multiplied by dictionary intensity.
- The Claude rater reports a confidence it states itself, not a calibrated probability.
- Regex topic routing has never been checked against human labels.
- The tweet gold queue puts the model's labels next to the human gold columns.

The paper measures sentiment toward court rulings, not stance toward a target, so its accuracy figures should not be read as an expected accuracy for CU stance.
works.question: Can few-shot prompts to large language models (GPT-3, GPT-4) be adapted, without task-specific training or large labeled sets, to political text-as-data tasks (sentiment classification, ad tone classification, ideology scaling, topic discovery), matching or beating conventional automated methods and approaching expert or crowd coding at far lower cost? The paper also asks what validation and prompt-design practices make such measures trustworthy.
works.method: Few-shot prompting. The LLM returns a next-word probability vector over labels, and continuous measures are built from it. Sentiment (tweets): six few-shot examples, two per class (positive, neutral, negative), with a preamble describing the ruling; the continuous measure is the first principal component of the probability vector (pre-registered via AsPredicted 92341, 92422, 92666, 100718, 125217; p.267-268). Ad tone: one-shot prompt (Figure 3), continuous tone from the probability vector. Ideology: one-shot Policy Prompt applied per sentence; sentence score = P(Conservative) minus P(Liberal); averaged to economic and social passage means per manifesto (p.273). GPT-4 ideology deviated from the pre-registered protocol and used the Le Mens and Gallego (2023) whole-document prompt (p.273). Topics: prompt asks GPT-3 for virtue labels; 51,483 labels returned, about 5-6 per speech, grouped by synonyms (p.275-276). Benchmarks: dictionary sentiment, Naive Bayes (bag of words), TweetNLP (RoBERTa fine-tuned on tweets, Camacho-Collados et al. 2022). Appendix A has zero-shot and one-shot variants (not in the text file).

findings.finding: Sentiment on 945 SCOTUS tweets: GPT-3 few-shot correctly predicts negative/positive in 88.4 percent of cases; TweetNLP 64.3 percent; best dictionary method 38.3 percent; Naive Bayes trained on 1.2M tweets 57.7 percent.

GPT-4 performs slightly worse than GPT-3 on the sentiment task; its probabilities are poorly calibrated and overconfident; for over 70 percent of posts GPT-4 gives a single-label probability above 99 percent; it returns Neutral more often than the authors.
findings.numbers: over 70% of posts with >99% probability

The LLM tone measure is said to correlate with expert ratings as strongly as the crowd measure; the text gives no coefficient for this.

findings.numbers: $0.60 vs $565.20; 935 ads; under 1 minute

findings.numbers: rho 0.92 economic; rho 0.8 social

Democrats more often praised advocacy (+3.5 pp), charity (+1.5), compassion (+3.9), education (+3.3), fairness (+3). related.why: Both papers use few-shot LLM coding checked against human labels. The persona channel code cites Birkenmaier and Lechner cue prompting (agency_communion_llm.py docstring). Ornstein does not cite Birkenmaier, and the Krippendorff-alpha role is not verified here.

Kim and Ornstein both apply few-shot GPT-class labelling to political text. Ornstein documents GPT-4 overconfidence on sentiment. Ornstein does not cite Kim. The 96.9 percent figure appears in the Kim item file but was not checked against Kim text.

Khan et al. compare fine-tuned RoBERTa with classical models for political tweet stance. Ornstein uses TweetNLP (a RoBERTa model) as the sentiment baseline that GPT-3 beats, 88.4 vs 64.3 percent. The tasks differ: Khan is stance, Ornstein is sentiment.

Rice and Zorn build corpus-specific dictionaries. Ornstein does not cite them and does not test corpus-specific dictionaries. Ornstein shows a general dictionary at 38.3 percent against GPT-3 at 88.4 percent on tweet sentiment, which bears on dictionary validity.

Haselmayer and Jenny combine a dictionary with crowd coding. Ornstein benchmarks LLM coding against crowd coding alone (Carlson and Montgomery 2017; Benoit et al. 2016), reporting about a 1000-fold cost reduction for 935 ad codings. The dictionary-plus-crowd route is not tested.
Both apply LLMs to political stance and sentiment classification. Dai adds logic-tensor constraints; Ornstein uses few-shot prompts with probability-vector outputs. Ornstein does not cite Dai.

works.title: The persuasive effects of political microtargeting in the age of generative artificial intelligence
works.summary: Simchon, Edwards and Lewandowsky (PNAS Nexus 2024, brief report) test whether matching a political ad's style to a reader's openness to experience raises perceived persuasiveness, and whether LLMs can mass-produce such matched ads. Four UK Prolific survey experiments (n = 440, 804, 803, 804) score each ad with a previously validated reader-side openness model and regress 1-5 perceived persuasion on person openness, ad openness and the mismatch |z(O_person) - z(O_ad)| in a mixed model with random intercepts for ads and participants. Mismatch lowers ratings with real Facebook ads (b = -0.07 and -0.08 per SD of mismatch) and with ChatGPT rewrites (b = -0.03, p < 0.001); GPT-3 rewrites miss significance (b = -0.01, p = 0.057). The authors call the effects small and convert them, by simulation on a midpoint cutoff, into 2,490 extra persuaded per 100,000 (median mismatch to none). The outcome is self-reported perceived persuasion, not attitude change or behaviour; only one trait is tested; reported t degrees of freedom do not square with the sample sizes, and study 2a/2b sample sizes are swapped between text and figure. For Paul's systems the paper is mostly a design contrast. Melange's receptivity layer treats Big Five traits as person-level main effects on susceptibility and seed probability, with no message-by-trait term, while this paper locates the effect in the interaction, above and beyond person openness. That is a modelling gap, not a recommendation: the population is the UK public rating ads, not legislators meeting lobbyists, the effects are small, and Melange's text-derived openness is its weakest trait. The paper's openness score also measures the appeal of text to open readers, a different construct from the author-trait openness Melange extracts from floor speech.
works.question: Does personality-congruent political messaging (ads matched to a reader's openness to experience) increase perceived persuasiveness, and can generative AI automate producing and validating such personalized ads at scale?
works.method: Linear mixed model predicting perceived persuasion from the participant's openness score, the ad's openness score and the matching score Matching_ij = |z(Openness_i) - z(Openness_j)|, with random intercepts for ads and participants. Study 2 generates low- and high-openness rewrites of each ad with GPT-3 or ChatGPT using a prompt containing the openness definition, an instruction and the original ad; openness of each ad scored by a previously validated language model (ref 13). Generated pairs with maximal openness difference selected, then run through the study 1 pipeline. Algorithmic validation via t-tests on generated ad openness scores; a smaller human-rater validation is reported in the supplement. Llama 2 70B replication of the algorithmic validation reported in the supplement.

findings.finding: Study 1a: larger personality mismatch lowers perceived persuasion (matching effect negative and significant), with real Facebook ads and 440 participants.
Study 1b: replication with 804 participants and the corrected 10-ad design shows the same negative matching effect.
Algorithmic validation: GPT-3 low- and high-openness rewrites differ in predicted openness in the expected direction, but the effect is small.
Algorithmic validation: ChatGPT rewrites differ in predicted openness in the expected direction, with a larger effect than GPT-3.
Study 2a (GPT-3-generated ads): matching effect narrowly fails conventional significance.
Study 2b (ChatGPT-generated ads): matching effect is significant; the authors say the more powerful model is what produced the significant effect.

related.why: Cited as ref 10 for microtargeting working even on a single attribute; Tappin measures persuasive returns to targeting with real attitude outcomes, a stronger test than this paper's perceived-persuasion ratings.
A systematic review of personality as a moderator of persuasion strategies; it places this paper's openness-matching result within the wider trait-by-message literature.
An agent-based model of why microtargeted campaigning pays at scale; it is the theoretical counterpart to this paper's argument that small per-person effects add up across 100,000 exposures.
Byrne supplies the person-level trait-to-susceptibility composite in Melange's receptivity layer; Simchon shows a message-by-trait interaction that a main-effects composite cannot capture.
A meta-analysis of inferring Big Five traits from digital footprints, the inference step this paper's manipulation machine assumes on the recipient side.
A meta-analysis of LIWC and Big Five links that bounds how much openness signal closed-vocabulary text carries, relevant to both this paper's text scoring and Melange's lexical O.

works.title: Pitch Perfect: Vocal Pitch and the Emotional Intensity of Congressional Speech
works.summary:
Dietrich, Hayes and O'Brien use 74,158 US House floor speeches from 2009 to 2014, each at least 50 words, taken from Clerk HouseLive audio. They measure each speech's mean vocal pitch (F0, extracted with Praat) and z-score it against the speaker's own baseline. They argue this is a hard-to-fake measure of arousal. It tracks intensity, not valence (footnote 1). Female members speak about 0.09 to 0.11 SD above their baseline when they mention women, while male members do not change (Table 1). Partisans speak about 0.29 to 0.38 SD higher on topics their party owns (Table 4). On days when many women speak with high pitch about women, male members mention women more, raise their own pitch on the topic, and co-vote more with the women speakers (Tables 5-7). These response results are observational, and the authors say they are not causal (p. 957).

The system has already built this method. `fec/members/b5_audio_descriptors_candidate.py:209-254` cites the paper by name and computes `pitch_deviation_from_speaker_baseline_z` and `topic_emotional_intensity`. The two differ in three ways. The paper relies on a cross-speaker contrast (female versus male, times topic) and roughly 120 speeches per speaker. The system reports a per-speaker topic mean with no comparison group. Its floors are 5 speech units per member, 2 topics, and 2 units per topic (`fec/audio_rules.py:20-22`). Effects of 0.1 to 0.4 SD cannot be detected at those floors. With only two topics, the sign of each topic's deviation is fixed by construction. The paper also measures in one floor venue with one channel. The system's baseline is pooled across interview programs and channels. The paper supports the system's existing rules: absolute F0 stays out of personality scores, and audio stays display-only. It also points to a better identity source: Clerk floor video, where the chamber has already identified the speaker.
works.question: Do small within-speaker deviations in vocal pitch (mean F0 relative to a speaker's own baseline) measure legislators' emotional intensity on an issue? Test case: do female House members speak with higher-than-baseline pitch when referencing women, compared with (a) male MCs on the same topic and (b) their own speech on other topics? Secondary questions: does pitch track issue commitments (women's interest-group scores; party-owned issues), and do emotionally intense female speeches about women relate to male MCs' subsequent speech and voting (p. 941-942, 944, 951)?
works.method: Pitch: mean fundamental frequency per speech extracted with Praat (Boersma 1993 algorithm; male floor 75 Hz, ceiling 300 Hz; female range 100-500 Hz), then z-scored within speaker so units are SD above/below each MC's baseline (p. 945-946; alternative Praat windows in SI S22-S30). Topic: binary indicator for any term in Pearson and Dancey (2011b) women dictionary; alternatives are word-share and a 30-topic structural topic model (STM) (p. 945-946). Models: multilevel logit for "Women mentioned" (Models 1.1-1.2, 5.1-5.2) and multilevel linear regression for standardized pitch with random intercepts per MC (Models 1.3-1.4, 4.x, 6.x); outcome models for Table 5, 6, 7 are multilevel logit/linear with day-level Female Speeches, Female Pitch and interactions (p. 946-956). Descriptive comparisons: Welch-type t-tests across speakers and groups (Table 2; Table 3 top-25 vs bottom-25 female MCs by pitch difference; t = 2.59, df = 48). Partisan issue test: Table 4 interaction of party with party-owned STM topics. Male voting outcome: proportion of votes cast with female speakers, standardized against each male MC's prior co-voting rate (p. 955-956). Predicted values from Models 5.2, 6.1 and 7.2 at female pitch +/-2 SD (p. 953-956).

findings.finding: Women are more likely than men to reference women in floor speeches.
findings.numbers: 17.82% of female speeches (2,403/13,484) vs 9.08% of male speeches (5,507/60,667); predicted probability 0.17 vs 0.08 (2.13 times). Holds with controls (Model 1.2).

findings.finding: Female MCs speak at higher-than-baseline pitch when referencing women, and male MCs do not.
findings.numbers: Female x 'Women mentioned' = 0.090 SD (SE 0.027, p<0.01) without controls and 0.112 SD (SE 0.027, p<0.01) with controls. Female MCs: +0.09 SD when referencing women, about five times the male change of +0.02 SD. Male pitch unchanged (t = 0.02, df 58,281). Democratic women t = 3.12; Republican women t = 2.81.

findings.finding: Raw pitch levels: female MCs' pitch rises on speeches mentioning women; male pitch is flat.
findings.numbers: Female MCs: 206.01 Hz when mentioning women vs 203.27 Hz otherwise. Male MCs: 151.50 Hz vs 151.49 Hz. Republican women 207.02 Hz vs Democratic women 205.68 Hz when mentioning women (not significantly different, fn 15).

findings.finding: Among female MCs, the most emotionally intense on women's issues have higher women's interest-group scores.
findings.numbers: Top 25 vs bottom 25 female MCs by pitch difference: difference in Vote Smart scores t = 2.59, df = 48, p < 0.02. Democratic women only: t = 2.83, df = 39, p <= 0.01. Republican women: t = 0.14, df = 7, not significant (small N). Table 3 group averages are not reliably extracted and are not relied on.

works.title: Potential and Pitfalls of Audio as Data for Political Research: Alignment, Features, and Classification Models
works.summary:
Mestre and Ryan (Political Analysis 2026) is a methods paper on audio as data. Its corpus is 45 U.S. presidential and VP debate videos (1960-2020; 47,150 transcript sentences). It runs four demonstrations. (1) Aeneas MFCC/DTW forced alignment, rated by crowd workers on 500 utterances x 5 ratings: percentage agreement 85.26%, distance agreement 95.76%, and about 5% of pairs not aligned at all, mostly short or interrupted sentences. (2) pYIN pitch and RMS energy. Energy is normalized by each debate's loudness, and within-speaker pitch deviation is shown over time. (3) Closed-set speaker identification. A single layer on mean-pooled wav2vec2-base embeddings reaches 0.914 accuracy across 156 speakers; a CNN on MFCCs reaches 0.081. (4) Off-the-shelf emotion models. The authors say these are biased by gender and pitch, and they disagree with expert coding.

For Melange the paper is less outside evidence than a method source. The speaker-identity research layer already copies it closely: `b5_audio_neural_head.py` reproduces the wav2vec2/Adam/batch-8/patience-3 head and cites section 4.3 and footnote 9, and `b5_audio_align_turns.py` uses Aeneas as the paper does. Melange's run of that same method on congressional audio failed. The fresh-21 neural EER was .226, against a bar of 5% or less. That run split train and test by source and event and used weak caption labels. The paper's 0.914 is in-domain debate audio, where the authors themselves warn that microphone placement and compression confound comparisons across speakers. So the paper's accuracy is not a benchmark Melange should expect to reach. The paper also backs the within-speaker pitch design and the fix for the sex confound in pitch variability. It cautions against the cross-member pooled eGeMAPS z-scores, which have no per-recording loudness or channel control. Its warnings about emotion models support keeping audio display-only.
works.question: Can audio be made usable as data for political research, given the "alignment crisis" (large text and audio corpora that do not intersect at the utterance level), and which audio features (LLDs, MFCCs, learned embeddings) and classifiers are useful for speech characterization, speaker identification, and emotion/valence measurement? The paper is a methods-and-applications demonstration; it does not test a substantive hypothesis.
works.method: Four applications of increasing complexity (Section 4, Table 2). (1) Forced alignment: aeneas, which matches MFCCs of the audio to synthetic-voice MFCCs via dynamic time warping; validated by human ratings on a 1-5 scale. (2) Speech characterization: pYIN pitch (F0) in 32 ms rolling windows and RMS energy per utterance, normalized by each debate's average loudness; within-speaker pitch deviations averaged over 5 s windows (Figure 3c). (3) Speaker identification: a custom CNN on MFCCs (two blocks of convolution, max-pooling and dropout) versus a single-layer neural network on 768-dimensional wav2vec2-base embeddings (Hugging Face facebook/wav2vec2-base); Adam, learning rate 0.001, cross-entropy loss, batch 32 (MFCC) or 8 (wav2vec2), early stopping with patience 3 (footnote 9). (4) Emotion: off-the-shelf models, not retrained: a SpeechBrain wav2vec2 model fine-tuned on IEMOCAP for four classes (anger, happiness, sadness, neutral), and Wagner et al. (2023) dimensional models for arousal, dominance and valence trained on MSP-Podcast. Text-based emotion and sentiment classifiers are compared with audio-based labels as a cross-check (Figure 4d).

works.title: Corpus-Based Dictionaries for Sentiment Analysis of Specialized Vocabularies
works.summary:
Rice and Zorn (2018, a PSRM revise-and-resubmit draft) argue that off-the-shelf sentiment dictionaries break on specialized vocabularies. Their alternative starts from 10 positive and 10 negative seed words, trains GloVe vectors on the domain corpus (300 dimensions, 50-token window, terms seen fewer than 90 times dropped), keeps the 500 nearest words on each side, weights counts by tf-idf and cosine similarity, and scores polarity as (Wp-Wn)/(Wp+Wn). On 50,000 IMDB reviews this reaches 80.4% in-sample and 79.5% held out, against about 69-71% for LIWC and AFINN. It needs roughly 5,000 or more documents before it beats them. On about 26,000 Supreme Court majority opinions (1792-2010), justice-level polarity ranks correlate only 0.29 with LIWC and 0.16 with AFINN, while those two correlate 0.64 with each other. The choice of dictionary therefore reorders the units. The paper calls its court validation suggestive, not conclusive, and notes that document-level polarity cannot say which subject the sentiment is about.

For Paul's system the sharpest point is Stage 5b. press_value = DEBATE stance sign x stock Lexicoder LSD2015 intensity. LSD lists "credit" as positive and "debt*", "charge*", "risk*", "oversight*" and "fraud*" as negative, and run_stage5.R scores every release with no masking of those domain terms. I ran a quick one-path check on 1,563 text-bearing releases (UNVERIFIED, per DE-062). It found the effect real but small: 4.5% of positive mass and 7.0% of negative mass come from those terms, the release-level intensity rank correlation is 0.953 with and without them, and the LSD net sign flips on 4.1% of releases. The legacy regex scorer cites Rice and Zorn for its polarity formula, but its lexicon is hand-weighted. Its corpus-expansion helper departs from the paper's parameters and was never run. The paper is a measurement template the press layer has not yet applied, not a reason to change rankings.
works.question: Can a "minimally-supervised" sentiment dictionary built from the corpus itself (seed words plus GloVe word-vector similarity) yield valid sentiment measures for specialized vocabularies where standard dictionaries (LIWC, AFINN) fail? The paper then applies the method to U.S. Supreme Court majority opinions to measure tone across 1792-2010, including over time and per justice.
works.method: Minimally-supervised dictionary construction. (1) Train GloVe word vectors (text2vec in R) on the corpus: 300 dimensions, Xmax = 10, context window 50 tokens, drop the 20 most frequent tokens, tokens in more than 90% of documents, and tokens appearing fewer than 90 times, with AdaGrad (p.6-9). (2) Seeds: 10 uncontroversial positive terms (e.g., "superb", "brilliant", "great") and 10 negative terms (e.g., "bad", "awful", "horrible") (fn.3, p.7). (3) Extract the top 500 positive and top 500 negative words by cosine similarity to the seed-sum vectors, removing SMART stop words and AFINN opposite-valence terms (fn.4, p.7-9). (4) Weight token counts by tf-idf and by cosine similarity to get similarity-weighted positive and negative counts (Wp, Wn). (5) Polarity = (sum Wp - sum Wn) / (sum Wp + sum Wn), centered and scaled for comparison (fn.6, p.8). Accuracy uses a zero cutpoint. Sensitivity tests: corpus size (Figure 2), number of extracted words (appendix), and temporal re-estimation. Validity: benchmark accuracy against assigned ratings (with comparison to LIWC, AFINN, and supervised baselines in Table 1), convergent validity (polarity vs. number of dissenting votes, Figure 3), and discriminant validity (justice-level differences from LIWC and AFINN, Figures 4-5).

findings.finding: Corpus-based dictionary polarity classifies movie reviews more accurately than standard dictionaries. In-sample accuracy is 80.4% (12,004 negative, 12,663 positive, 332 neutral) versus 69.4% for LIWC (with scaling) and 71.3% for AFINN.
findings.numbers: 80.4% vs 69.4% (LIWC) vs 71.3% (AFINN); 12,004 neg / 12,663 pos / 332 neutral

findings.finding: Out-of-sample (held-out 25,000 reviews) accuracy is consistent with in-sample accuracy: 79.5% for the corpus-based approach, 69.7% for LIWC, and 70.6% for AFINN.
findings.numbers: 79.5% (ours, held-out) vs 69.7% (LIWC) vs 70.6% (AFINN)

findings.finding: Accuracy gains hold across corpus sizes. Even 5,000-document corpora beat the LIWC and AFINN accuracy figures, and accuracy approaches standard machine-learning levels by about 15,000 documents. Accuracy rises with corpus size, with diminishing returns after about 30,000.
findings.numbers: 5,000 docs beats 69.4%/71.3%; ~15,000 docs reaches roughly 80%; mean review 184 tokens (max 2,085)

findings.finding: Compared with supervised classifiers on the same movie-review benchmark, the approach matches Naive Bayes, MaxEnt, and SVM (about 79-80%) but falls short of Pang and Lee (2004, 87.15%) and Maas et al. (2011, 88.05%). The paper stresses it uses no classification labels.
findings.numbers: Ours 80.4; Pang, Lee and Vaithyanathan (2002) NB 79.7, MaxEnt 79.7, SVM 79.4 (mean); Pang and Lee 2004 87.15; Maas et al. 2011 88.05

findings.finding: Dictionaries estimated on temporal subsets of the Court's opinions differ sharply. Only 34.0% of negative and 27.7% of positive terms carry over from the early Court to the turn-of-century Court; only 24.2% of negative and 19.6% of positive terms carry over from the turn-of-century Court to the modern Court.
findings.numbers: 34.0% neg / 27.7% pos (early to turn-of-century); 24.2% neg / 19.6% pos (turn-of-century to modern)

findings.finding: Convergent validity: only the corpus-based polarity measure declines consistently as the number of dissenting votes rises. LIWC and AFINN show increases in polarity at various points, most notably in 6-3 decisions. In the modern era, the corpus-based measure treats unanimous opinions as generally positive.

works.title: Machine and deep learning for personality traits detection: a comprehensive survey and open research challenges
works.summary:
Naz et al. (2025) is a survey of machine-learning and deep-learning methods that detect personality from text. It covers 171 studies, selected from 305 search hits by a screening funnel whose numbers do not add up. It sorts methods into shallow ML, ensembles, sequential deep learning and transformers, catalogues 14 text datasets (several of them no longer available), and runs one experiment on the Kaggle MBTI data. In that experiment, Bi-LSTM with sentence embeddings (Extraversion 92, Agreeableness 91) and DistilBERT (Openness 92, Conscientiousness 91) beat TF-IDF SVM (Openness 89, Conscientiousness 80).

The empirical part is weak. It reports accuracy only, with no train/test split, cross-validation, class balance or variance. It reports Big Five traits on a dataset labeled with MBTI types and never explains the mapping. Its text and tables disagree in several places. Its Table 9 ranks results from different papers as if they used the same data and protocol. The authors' answer to their research questions is that transformers and deep embeddings perform best, while traditional ML stays interpretable and competitive on small data.

For Paul's system the paper is mostly context. Its population is ordinary social-media users who labeled their own personality type. The system instead measures legislators' public speech and checks it against expert and insider panels and against the Ramey, Klingler and Hollibaugh (RKH) congressional estimates, using single-look held-out correlations. The paper's accuracy figures are not comparable to the system's held-out r (mean .350 vs RKH) and should not be quoted as benchmarks. Two points do carry over. First, the paper states that personality datasets do not directly measure emotional stability or neuroticism, which matches the system's record that no gold criterion exists for N. Second, its finding that classical TF-IDF models stay competitive on small labeled sets matches the stance stack's measured result: LinearSVC at 83.9% beat the transformer at 0.757 on 87 test rows. That second point tempers Paul's view that bag-of-words SVMs are outdated.
works.question: Six research questions (Sec 3, p.3; answered in Sec 13, pp.45-46): RQ1 Which ML models suit personality trait detection in online text? RQ2 Which DL models suit it? RQ3 How do diverse features and ML/DL models affect accuracy? RQ4 What features and dataset sources exist? RQ5 What application areas exist and how do they affect fields? RQ6 What open research challenges exist and what strategies address them?
works.method: Systematic-style review: keyword search strings (p.6, Table 3 p.10), duplicate and title screening, abstract screening, full review, and quality questions on domain and venue (p.7; criteria not reported in detail). Taxonomy by shallow ML, ensemble, sequential DL (RNN/CNN/LSTM/Bi-LSTM/GRU), and transformers (Sec 7, pp.11-20; Tables 5-8). Preprocessing: lowercasing, URL/punctuation/number removal, stop-word removal, lemmatization and stemming, tokenization (Sec 7.1, pp.11-13; Sec 9.1, p.25). Features: TF-IDF, POS tags, BoW, N-grams, Word2Vec, GloVe, FastText, sentence embeddings (Sec 7.2, pp.13-14; Sec 9.2, p.26). Models: SVM, NB, LR, DT, KNN, GB, RF, XGBoost, AdaBoost, LSTM, Bi-LSTM, BERT, DistilBERT (Sec 9.3, pp.26-27). Empirical comparison is tabulated accuracy only (Tables 10-12).

works.title: Automatic construction of direction-aware sentiment lexicon using direction-dependent words
works.summary:
Park, Lee and Cho build a financial sentiment lexicon in which each entry pairs a directional word ("up" or "down" family) with a noun whose polarity depends on that direction. Their example is "cost", which is negative alone but positive in "cost decrease". Sentences in the Financial PhraseBank are tagged proportional or inversely proportional from an up-count minus down-count score. PMI between nouns and the two tags picks out 56 direction-dependent words, and these yield 1,767 pairs. Adding the pairs to Loughran-McDonald raises weighted F1 on the PhraseBank subsets from about 0.59-0.62 to 0.71-0.82. On SemEval and FiQA it stays below 0.5, and fine-tuned RoBERTa is far ahead (about 0.96 on DS100). The construction set was heavily imbalanced (28 inversely proportional sentences against 691 proportional), which produced noisy words. Evaluation covers headline-length sentences only, with no significance tests.

This paper has already been used in Paul's system. The brain notes say he adapted it as a "directional verb x CU-valenced target" override for the CFPB sign-flip problem. A whole-text version made 46 sign changes on gold: 3 good and 43 bad. It was rejected because releases defending the CFPB describe the attack with "shrink" verbs. The idea that survives in the built system is a curated, direction-separated target registry (cfpb_reform +1, cfpb_expansion -1, cfpb_institution 0), not an automatic lexicon. The paper explains both results. Its pairs work on short headlines where the direction word modifies the noun, and press releases are long, multi-actor texts. The paper's own failure cases (pairs like company/increase) and its class imbalance match the churn seen in Paul's dry run. The open question in the system (restrict the rule to the sentence or headline that names the bill) is the condition under which the paper's evidence would actually transfer. Nothing here concerns networks, money or allocation.
works.question: Can a financial sentiment lexicon be built automatically so that each entry is a pair of a directional word (up/down) and a direction-dependent word, so that sentiment flips correctly with direction (e.g., "cost" negative, but "cost decrease" positive)? Does adding these pairs to the Loughran-McDonald (LM) word list improve sentence-level sentiment classification of financial headlines? (Sect. 1, pp. 845-846)
works.method: Stage 1 (direction tagging, Sect. 3.1): each polar sentence gets a direction score = count of "up" words minus count of "down" words (Porter stemming, NLTK). Sentences are tagged "proportional" (positive with score > 0, or negative with score < 0) or "inversely proportional" (the reverse). Neutral sentences are excluded. Stage 2 (association, Sect. 3.2): nouns are lemmatized (NLTK); nouns occurring in fewer than 1% of sentences are dropped. PMI(w,t) = log2 [p(w,t) / (p(w) p(t))] is computed for each noun and tag. Dependency score (Eq. 1) keeps PMI(w,tp) if PMI(w,tp) - PMI(w,ti) > delta, uses -PMI(w,ti) if the difference is below -delta, and 0 otherwise; delta = 0 in this study. Stage 3 (extraction, Sect. 3.3): from each sentence, the highest-scoring proportional word or the lowest-scoring inversely proportional word is kept as the direction-dependent word; words with non-alphabetic characters or fewer than k = 3 letters are removed. Stage 4 (Senti-DD, Sect. 3.4): pairs of directional and direction-dependent words are labelled positive-context or negative-context. Stage 5 (evaluation, Sect. 4.2): LM sentiment score = PosScore - NegScore (Eq. 2); ContextScore = ContPosScore - ContNegScore (Eq. 3); RefinedScore = SentimentScore + ContextScore (Eq. 4); sign of the refined score gives positive, neutral or negative. Baselines: Sentiment140, SentiWordNet, SO-CAL, MPQA, TextBlob, VADER, SentiStrength, AFINN, LM. Pretrained comparators: Word2Vec with logistic regression (word2vec-google-news-300), BERT-base-uncased and RoBERTa-base fine-tuned (Adam, weight decay 0.01, batch 8, 500 warm-up steps, 3 epochs; Sect. 4.4, pp. 856-857). Hyperparameters were set heuristically, and the authors state that tuning is left to future work (p. 857).

On the SemEval and FiQA sets, LM+Senti-DD is still below 0.5 F1 (0.4789 SemEval; 0.4937 FiQA). Pretrained models do better on nearly all measures, and the authors attribute this to lexicon methods needing explicit sentiment words.
