works.title: Sentiment analysis of political communication: combining a dictionary approach with crowdcoding
works.summary:
Haselmayer and Jenny build a negativity dictionary for German-language Austrian political text. About 480 CrowdFlower coders rated 12,713 sentences on a 0-4 negativity scale, ten ratings per sentence, for about 2,000 EUR. Each word's score is the mean score of the sentences it appears in, which yields 5,001 lemmatized words. To score a new sentence, the method takes its single most negative dictionary word (the max rule). A negator drops the word that follows it, and an intensifier multiplies a word's score by 1.25.

Validation on 200 sentences:
- The averaged lay crowd agrees with expert coding at r = 0.82.
- The dictionary agrees with experts at r = 0.65, matching 84% of sentences.
- On 755 statements coded by a single expert, the dictionary gives r = 0.63 at 82% coverage.
- Two translated general-purpose German dictionaries score r = 0.13 and 0.19. The authors read this as evidence that a domain-built dictionary is needed.
- Preprocessing and aggregation choices move r from 0.13 to 0.65.
- In a regression on the 2013 campaign, dictionary scores keep the expert-coded signs but shrink the effects. The government-pair coefficient is -0.13 with the dictionary versus -0.40 with expert coding.

The paper matters here in two places:
1. The live press intensity is stock English Lexicoder LSD2015, scored per release as |net| / words. Its only recorded validation is a three-case smoke test, and it has never been compared with human-coded intensity. The paper's design would supply that test cheaply.
2. Paul's retired graded tone scorer cites this paper by name, but its code departs from the paper. It sums weighted cues across sentences where the paper takes the strongest cue, uses a two-token negator window, adds a downtoner, and uses about 45 hand-weighted patterns rather than crowd-derived word scores.

The evidence is about Austrian German, covers negativity only, and comes from 2013. None of it validates the US congressional tone measures directly.
works.question: Can a negative sentiment dictionary for a language and domain of choice be built cheaply through crowdcoding, and does its word-based tonality score validly measure fine-grained negativity relative to expert and crowd coding? The authors illustrate use with (a) negative campaigning among Austrian parties in the 2013 national election and (b) media tonality toward parties and candidates.
works.method: Five-step procedure (Sec. 4): (1) sample sentences containing seed negative words; (2) crowdcode each sentence on a 0-4 negativity scale (0 not negative to 4 very strongly negative) plus an "uncodable" option, with test questions (4 initial, 1 in 5 later; two adjacent categories accepted); coders below 75% test accuracy excluded; (3) sentence score = mean of 10 coder ratings; (4) word score = mean of sentence scores in which the word occurs; word forms lemmatized with TreeTagger and POS-tagged, with manual post-processing; (5) remove words under 3 characters, high-frequency function words, names of persons, parties and organizations (AUTNES list), positive words from existing lexicons, and words occurring in only one sentence. Scoring of new texts (Sec. 5): bag-of-words; sentence tonality = most negative dictionary word (max rule); negation word immediately before a dictionary word excludes that word (no polarity flip); intensifier before a word multiplies its score by 1.25, capped at the scale maximum. Validation (Sec. 6, App. 2-3): Pearson correlations with expert and crowd means, coverage, and comparison with two translated German dictionaries (SentiWS, Momtazi). Applications: OLS regression of press-release tonality with government/opposition and coalition-pair indicators, party fixed effects, poll-performance and days-to-election controls, standard errors clustered by party pair (Table 3); descriptive comparison of mean sentence tonality with and without an actor reference, by day (Sec. 7.2, Fig. 6).

findings.finding: Crowd sentence scores: 480 coders passed the tests with 92% mean accuracy (SD 0.07); about 130,000 valid codings, ten per sentence, for 12,713 sentences; the test-question design implies a 4% chance of passing by guessing.
findings.numbers: 480 coders; 92% (SD 0.07); ~130,000 codings; 12,713 sentences; ~2,000 EUR (~2,200 USD)

findings.finding: Dictionary scope and size: the rated bag of words falls from about 40,000 initial words to about 5,000 after removing short, frequent, rare, positive, and named-entity words.
findings.numbers: 5,001 dictionary words; scores 0.06-3.8 on the 0-4 scale; mean 2.04 (SD 0.65)

findings.finding: Lay crowd aggregates replicate expert coding of the 200-sentence test sample, with a slight centrist bias.
findings.numbers: Pearson r = 0.82 (aggregated expert vs aggregated crowd, n = 200)

findings.finding: Dictionary validity against expert coding: a moderate correlation at 84% coverage. Setting the 32 uncovered sentences to zero lowers the correlation.
findings.numbers: r = 0.65, coverage 84% (n = 200); r = 0.6 after assigning zero to 32 uncovered sentences

findings.finding: Replication on a larger sample: single expert coding of 755 statements gives similar coverage and correlation; the dictionary-based estimates are described as more conservative than manual-coding estimates.
findings.numbers: n = 755; coverage 82%; r = 0.63

findings.finding: Generic German dictionaries perform far worse on the same sample, which the authors take as evidence that customization is needed.
findings.numbers: Momtazi: r = 0.13, coverage 46%; SentiWS: r = 0.19, coverage 31%; political dictionary: r = 0.65, coverage 84%

related.why: Both argue for domain-specific sentiment dictionaries. Rice and Zorn derive one from the corpus with word vectors; this paper derives one from crowd ratings. The legacy scorer cites both papers. Verified against the Rice item's research question.

Merkley and Stecula use Lexicoder with a custom dictionary to detect party cues, not to measure sentiment intensity. The link is a method precedent for custom dictionaries, not a validation of tone. Verified against the Merkley item text.

Also a domain-lexicon construction method. The rejected bill-sign-handling test (3 good / 43 bad) is claimed in the analyst text and was not checked here; the link rests on the shared point that preprocessing and aggregation choices drive validity.
Offers LLM few-shot coding of political text as an alternative to the crowdcoding step used for intensity gold labels. Verified against the Ornstein item research question.

works.title: Learning Personalised Models for Automatic Self-Reported Personality Recognition
works.summary: Salam, Manoranjan, Jiang and Celiktutan (PMLR 173, 2022) ask whether one Big Five recognizer for everyone is worse than separate models for each user profile. They test this on UDIVA dyadic video (188 interactions, 147 participants, 90.5 hours, mostly Spanish speakers). For each profile (female/male; age 30 or under/over 30) and each modality, they run an Auto-Keras architecture search. Modalities are face/body landmarks, talk-turn duration, content, sentiment and speech rate, SBERT text and MFCC audio. Predictions are then fused at the decision level. The outcome is self-reported OCEAN, scored by mean squared error. Fusing the two best modalities within each gender gives an average MSE of 0.690. Age-wise fusion gives 0.796 and generic fusion 0.818. Dyadformer scores 0.722 and the authors' earlier challenge ensemble 0.769. Almost all of the gain comes from the gender split. Age adds little, and in the generic setting fusion barely beats the best single modality (0.818 vs 0.820). Turn-taking features beat face/body features (0.874 vs 1.325). The evidence is thin. There is one challenge test split, with no test N, subgroup sizes, intervals or seed variance. Gender is binary, the fairness claim is untested, and the text and Table 1 disagree on the headline number. For Paul's systems, the transferable lesson is narrow. Acoustic features whose signal partly is speaker sex need sex-conditioned comparison. The Melange audio lane already ran a Salam-style check: pace and volume are sex-clean, while pitch variability and jitter are not. But the semitone-SD fix sits on an unmerged branch. The paper gives no basis for building per-sex trait models for legislators, whose criteria are expert ratings, not self-reports. All transfer here is UNVERIFIED.
works.question: Does learning separate neural architectures per user profile (gender, or age split at 30) improve automatic self-reported Big Five personality recognition over one generic model, using multimodal behavioural features from dyadic interactions?
works.method: Per-modality features: FaceBody landmark mean and SD (552 dims); talk-turn duration (5), content (5), sentiment (10, Spanish-only library), speech rate (5); SBERT sentence embeddings; MFCC-20 band-energy statistics. For each profile (female, male; age 30 or under, over 30) and each modality, Auto-Keras neural architecture search (network morphism with Bayesian optimisation), 100 trials, up to 1,000 epochs, Adam optimiser, MSE loss, early stopping patience 30, 85/15 train/validation split, default start of two 32-unit dense layers. Decision fusion: per-minute scores averaged over sessions, then modality predictions averaged, using the best two modalities or all modalities. Comparison against generic models and challenge-team results.

findings.finding: Gender-wise bimodal NAS (fusion of two best modalities) gives the lowest AMSE in the paper; generic and age-wise bimodal fusion are higher.
findings.numbers: AMSE 0.690 gender-wise; 0.796 age-wise; 0.818 generic fusion

findings.finding: Abstract's error reduction is measured against generic bimodal fusion, not the generic best single modality.
findings.numbers: Reduction 0.128 vs generic fusion; generic best single modality 0.820, so gap 0.130

findings.finding: In the generic setting, bimodal fusion barely improves on the best single modality; the gain is concentrated in the gender split.
findings.numbers: Generic fusion 0.818 vs best single 0.820; gender fusion 0.690 vs gender best single 0.695

findings.finding: Age-wise personalisation helps only slightly over the generic model.
findings.numbers: Age-wise fusion 0.796 vs generic fusion 0.818

findings.finding: Against the challenge comparison, gender-wise bimodal NAS beats Dyadformer and the authors' prior winning ensemble on AMSE.
findings.numbers: Gender bimodal 0.690; Dyadformer 0.722; prior SMART-SAIR ensemble 0.769; challenge baseline 0.818

findings.finding: Per-trait results for gender-wise bimodal NAS; it beats the prior ensemble on all traits except Agreeableness, where the prior ensemble is ahead by 0.002.

works.title: Big Five Personality Predictions From Twitter Using Regression
works.summary:
**What the paper is.** This is a short SSRN proposal from a student engineering group at MIET College, Meerut. It describes a pipeline that would take a Twitter handle, clean and tokenize the tweets, and build TF-IDF, LIWC-style, sentiment and profile features (follower count, tweet frequency, bio). A classifier or regression would then output each Big Five trait as a percentage, shown in a pie chart. The paper reports no sample size, no data period, no source for its trait labels, and no accuracy figures. The model list changes between sections. The trait names are non-standard ("Creativity, Dependability, Sociability, Kindness, Anxiety"), and several citations do not match the reference list. The abstract's claim about stress detection has no method behind it. In short, this is a design sketch, not evidence.

**Why it matters here, and how little.** The only component it touches is Melange's lexical Big Five reader. That reader already does more than the paper proposes: LIWC-analog rates, Mairesse SMOreg weights, a refit to RKH targets, token-based low-confidence shrinkage, and reported held-out CV (mean .350 across the five traits, window and N as recorded in the brain). The project's validation record goes further still. The pre-registered nomological look rated lexical Big Five as unfit for behavioural prediction, and receptivity now runs on a behavioural basis. The paper offers nothing that could test or recalibrate any of this, and none of its features should be adopted on its authority. Two cautions transfer. First, its profile features (follower count, tweet frequency) are volume proxies of the kind the system has already rejected. Second, it outputs absolute "percentages" with no reference norm, while the system deliberately reports traits as z-scores relative to its own corpus. Read it as a negative example of an unvalidated trait-from-text claim, not as support.
works.question: Can the Big Five personality traits of a Twitter user be predicted automatically from their tweets using NLP, sentiment analysis and machine learning/regression, as a scalable alternative to questionnaire-based assessment? (Abstract; Section 1.) The text never states a formal hypothesis.
works.method: Pipeline (Sections 3.1-3.6): (1) cleaning, removing URLs, mentions, hashtags, lowercasing and stopword removal; (2) tokenization; (3) TF-IDF vectorization, plus LIWC and other psycholinguistic features; (4) user profile features (follower count, tweet frequency, bio); (5) sentiment analysis of positive and negative tone; (6) classifiers named as Random Forest, Neural Networks and SVM (Section 3.3), and elsewhere Naive Bayes, SVM, RNN or BERT (Section 3.5 text), with supervised regression to output a percentage per Big Five trait (Sections 1, 3.5, Figure 5). Training uses cross-validation to limit overfitting. Evaluation uses accuracy, precision, recall and confusion matrices (Section 3.4). Feature importance is analysed (Section 3.5). The results are visualised as pie charts (Abstract; Section 4). Regression is described only in words and in Figure 5 (caption only). The paper contains no equations beyond the TF-IDF formula caption (Figure 2).

works.title: Getting Personal: A Deep Learning Artifact for Text-Based Measurement of Personality
works.summary: Yang, Lau and Abbasi (ISR 2023) build DeepPerson, a design-science artifact for Big Five detection from text. It stacks an ELMo-style CNN-LSTM encoder (one Bi-LSTM for syntax and semantics, one for LIWC/MRC/SPLICE concept embeddings), a word-layer-person hierarchical attention network (wlpHAN), and SPDFiT, a Bayesian pseudo-labeling fine-tuner whose entropy quality score both filters pseudo-labels and scales the learning rate. Labels are self-report Big Five median-split to binary. On PANDORA (Reddit, 1,568 users) DeepPerson reaches AUC 75.0 vs 64.6 for the best comparator (AttRCNN), 63.4 PersonaBERT, 61.5 BERT-Base, and roughly 56 for the IBM feature-based baseline; on myPersonality (Facebook, 250 users) AUC 70.7 vs 63.3. Essays-corpus results sit in an appendix not in the text file. Ablations credit SPDFiT most, wlpHAN about 5 pp, and the LIWC-type concept encoder about 2 pp. Downstream, adding DeepPerson scores to GBDT forecasts of eight Compustat outcomes for 352 S&P 1500 executives with Twitter accounts cuts MSE by 14.29% on average (RFR 6.67%); this is framed as prediction, not causation, and executive-level scores are never validated against surveys. For Melange the paper is a benchmark showing that closed-vocabulary linear scoring, which the lexical Big Five uses, is the weakest family on self-report criteria, while LIWC concepts still add signal inside a deep model. It does not touch legislators, elite speech genres, observer or gold-panel criteria, or lobbying responsiveness, so its accuracy numbers are UNSTRATIFIED by genre and population relative to the system, and nothing here is reproduced (UNVERIFIED per DE-062).
works.question: RQ1: Relative to existing NLP methods, how effectively can DeepPerson detect personality dimensions from user-generated text? RQ2: Can enhanced personality measurement significantly improve downstream forecasting outcomes? (p. 195)
works.method: DeepPerson artifact has three parts: (a) CNN-LSTM encoder: CNN character encoder, word CNN embeddings, two multilayer Bi-LSTMs (ELMo-style, pretrained on 1B Word), one for syntax/semantics and one for LIWC/MRC/SPLICE psychological concept embeddings, aggregated to 1,024-dim (Eqs. 1-3, pp. 200-202); (b) wlpHAN, word-layer-person hierarchical attention with layer attention (Eq. 4), word attention (Eq. 6), and a person-level Bi-LSTM (Eq. 7), softmax over Big Five categories (Eqs. 8-9, pp. 202-204); (c) SPDFiT, self-taught fine-tuning: Bayesian pseudo-labeling with Gaussian class-conditional priors, entropy-based quality score s_m in [0,1] that both filters and scales SGD learning rate (Algorithm 1, p. 206; Section 3.3, pp. 204-206). Implemented on ELMo in PyTorch; mini-batch 500, dropout 0.5, grid search on validation users. Metrics: macro-averaged F, precision, recall, accuracy, AUC; Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Downstream: Big Five scores as features added to baseline features in random forest regression (RFR) and gradient boosted decision trees (GBDT), scikit-learn, 20 estimators; comparators CNN-1, CNN-2, BERT, PersonaBERT, and ARIMA; outcomes measured as the log of the first two-year average after executive entry; improvement = (MSE_baseline - MSE_experimental)/MSE_baseline; Wilcoxon tests (p. 215-216).

findings.finding: On PANDORA, DeepPerson reaches AUC 75.0 vs. best comparators AttRCNN 64.6, CNN-1 64.0, PersonaBERT 63.4; macro F 65.1 vs AttRCNN 59.5. Text says DeepPerson beats best comparators by 5-15 pp across measures.
findings.numbers: AUC 75.0; Imp. +33.7% vs IBM baseline; AttRCNN AUC 64.6 (+15.2%)

findings.finding: On myPersonality, DeepPerson reaches AUC 70.7 vs AttRCNN 63.3 and PersonaBERT 61.2; macro F 67.0 vs 59.0 for AttRCNN. Wilcoxon tests significant (p<0.01) vs CNN-1 on most traits.

SPDFiT is the largest single contributor. Removing wlpHAN drops AUC by about 5 pp. Replacing SPDFiT with UDA, Self-Ensembling, logistic/Lasso/Ridge pseudo-labeling, or BERT variants lowers AUC from 70.0 to 58.3-65.2. Ablation is on PANDORA.
findings.numbers: CNN-LSTM (SPDFiT) AUC 70.0 (+20.1%); 1BWord only 62.3; UDA 65.1; Self-Ensembling 65.2; Logistic 64.9; BERT-Base 60.2; PersonaBERT 63.4; Doc2Vec 58.3

findings.finding: SPDFiT still beats comparators when only part of the unlabeled data is used: about 50% of unlabeled data gives fairly good results, and SPDFiT outperforms all alternatives at 40%+ of PANDORA or 30%+ of myPersonality unlabeled data.

Full wlpHAN AUC 70.3 vs AttRCNN 64.6, HCAN 61.1, HAN 60.7, Msg-Attn 60.5; text reports 3-6 pp lift over those networks and 5-11% relative gains (all p<0.01). Each of the syntax/semantic, concept, and person encoders adds about 2 pp (text claim).

works.title: Using Linguistic Cues for the Automatic Recognition of Personality in Conversation and Text
works.summary: Mairesse, Walker, Mehl and Moore (JAIR 30, 2007) is the source of the SMOreg personality models that Ramey, Klingler and Hollibaugh ran on congressional floor speech. Those RKH estimates are the targets the lexical Big Five weights are now fitted to. The paper trains classifiers, regressors and RankBoost rankers on LIWC, MRC, speech-act and prosody features. It uses two corpora: 2,479 student essays with self-reports, and 96 EAR speakers with self-reports plus averaged ratings from 18 observers. Three results bear on the system. (1) On essays the signal is weak. In regression, only openness (r 0.33) and emotional stability (r 0.24) beat the mean baseline, and SMOreg is significant only for openness (Table 17). The system's 07-03 essays refit landed in the same weak band and was later replaced by the RKH refit. (2) Ramey footnote 4 says RKH used the observer-trained models, which are the EAR models with n = 96. In Table 19, SMOreg on EAR observer ratings is worse than predicting the mean for every trait, with relative errors from 131.75 to 213.20 percent. The reference instrument behind the held-out r of .350 against RKH therefore had no demonstrated out-of-sample accuracy in its own paper. (3) Observer-rated personality is easier to model than self-report in conversation, and emotional stability has the lowest inter-observer agreement (pair r .29). This fits the system's choice of observer gold panels and its weak N results. Prosody helps extraversion most. In self-reports, neuroticism goes with low, constant voice intensity, which supports the 2026-07-09 finding that the audio ES composite was mis-signed. No result here was reproduced by a second path, so the bearings are UNVERIFIED (DE-062).
works.question: Can the Big Five personality traits be recognised automatically from linguistic cues in written essays and in conversation, using self-reports and observer ratings, and which model type (classification, regression or ranking) and feature set performs best? Sec 1.
works.method: Supervised learning with Weka and 10-fold cross-validation. Classification: each trait split into two equal-size bins; six learners (J48, 1-NN, Naive Bayes, JRip, AdaBoostM1, linear SVM SMO) vs majority-class baseline (Sec 4). Regression: linear regression, M5' regression tree, M5' model tree, REPTree, SVM regression vs mean baseline, scored by relative absolute error (Sec 5). Ranking: RankBoost with 100 boosting rounds trained on ordered pairs from two individuals, indicator functions from thresholded feature values, loss = share of misordered pairs; random baseline 0.50 (Sec 6). Feature-set ablations for each model type; interpretation via decision trees, rules and regression trees (Sec 4.3, 5.3, 6.3). Pearson correlations of features with ratings (p<0.05) in Sec 3.3, Tables 8-11. Speech acts tagged by heuristic parse rules (Sec 3.2.2).
findings: Essays, self-reports, binary (two equal bins), 10-fold CV: SMO best. Openness 62.1 percent vs 50.3 baseline; emotional stability 57.4 percent; conscientiousness hardest, about 55 percent with only two classifiers significant. Table 12, p.475.

EAR, observer ratings, binary: Naive Bayes reaches 73.0 percent for extraversion (baseline 47.8), 73.9 percent for emotional stability (baseline 51.1), 67.7 percent for conscientiousness and 61.3 percent for agreeableness. Openness not significant. Table 14, p.476-477.
EAR, self-reports: no classifier significantly beats the baseline (Table 14), and no regression self-report model does either (Sec 5.2, p.482).

EAR observer feature sets, Naive Bayes: prosody alone 67.6 percent for extraversion and LIWC alone 68.9 percent, both below the full-set 73.0 percent; MRC alone best for conscientiousness (66.8 percent); prosody alone best for openness (64.6 percent). Table 15, p.477.

Essays, binary: LIWC features beat MRC features for every trait; LIWC alone gives 62.5 percent for openness, and LIWC alone performs slightly better than the full feature set. Table 13 and Sec 4.1, p.476.
Essays, regression, self-reports: openness relative error 93.3 percent (M5 model tree, Pearson r 0.33) and emotional stability 96.4 percent (r 0.24); other traits not significant. Table 17, p.480.

related.why: Ramey et al. apply the pre-trained Mairesse SMOreg to floor speech (text lines 130 and 183-190). Their footnote 4 says observer-trained models; footnote 8 says SMOreg versus M5 made little difference. Their line 191 calls the training sample essay, so the provenance is inconsistent within Ramey.
Review of LIWC and personality language. It shares the LIWC dictionary with this paper but does not supply the essays data, which is Pennebaker and King 1999 (cited, not in this review).
Meta-analysis of 52 LIWC categories against the Big Five that reports small effect sizes. This supports the point about small closed-vocabulary signal; the paper does not cite Mairesse 2007.
Online appendix to expert evaluations of senators. The link to this paper is conceptual (observer or expert ratings); the appendix does not mention Mairesse 2007.
Personalised models for self-reported personality recognition. It does not cite Mairesse 2007, so the link is topical only; the rel labelled it extends, which is not supported.
Cites Mairesse 2007 as reference 179 and calls it the foundation of personality computing with accuracy below 62 percent. Celli discusses threats in general, not Mairesse-specific validity threats.

works.title: Stance Detection: A Practical Guide to Classifying Political Beliefs in Text
works.summary: Burnham's methods guide treats stance as textual entailment: a document's stance is how its author would answer a stated proposition. Stance is kept separate from sentiment. The guide compares three ways to classify it on about 2,135 human-coded Trump-approval tweets and newsletter sentences, scored by MCC. Supervised models: bag-of-words gets 0.49 to 0.51 and transformers 0.60 to 0.68. Zero-shot NLI: DeBERTaV3 Base gets 0.40 and Large 0.65. In-context LLMs: GPT-4 gets 0.78, or 0.80 with logit bias, but costs $12.52 per run and cannot be archived. The main practical finding is about context. Human coders disagree more when the target is not named (34.0% versus 19.5%), and NLI degrades most in that case. When outside knowledge is needed, supervised or in-context classifiers do better. The guide recommends NLI as the reproducible default. LLMs are fine for expanding training data or for validation, but not as the main source of labels. The arXiv text is v2. An online check confirms the published version in PSRM 13 (2025), 611-628, online September 2024. This bears directly on Paul's CU press-stance stack, which runs Burnham's own Political DEBATE base model (a later, politics-trained NLI model) as its main reader. The system's own history repeats the paper's context finding. Zero-shot DEBATE missed implicit anti-CU stances (oppose F1 0.08), and fine-tuning on 552 labels fixed this. The paper also highlights three things the system has not settled: model size (base versus large), labels that fall back to Claude pre-labels, and the lack of an MCC or hypothesis-wording check. All system-side figures are the project's own reports, measured on small held-out sets (n = 87 or 156). They are UNVERIFIED by a second path.
works.question: How should political scientists define and operationalize stance detection (the position a document expresses toward a proposition), and which classification approach (supervised, NLI zero-shot, or in-context generative LLM) should they choose given document context, compute, reproducibility and human labor constraints? A secondary aim is to show that NLI and in-context classifiers can replicate a supervised-classifier finding on COVID-19 mitigation stance (Block Jr et al. 2022).
works.method: Three classifier families compared. (1) Supervised: bag-of-words logistic regression, random forest and SVM (grid search) versus RoBERTa, BERTweet, PoliBERTweet and DeBERTaV3 base (Bayesian hyperparameter sweep, 10 runs each; MCC primary metric; pp.11-12). (2) NLI zero-shot: DeBERTaV3 Large NLI model; each tweet paired with hypothesis templates (single versus multi-hypothesis; keyword matching of hypotheses to documents; 9 synonymous hypotheses for sensitivity; pp.14-15). (3) In-context: GPT-4, GPT-3.5 Turbo and Zephyr 7B with system and user prompts, temperature 0, zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought and logit bias variants (Table 5, pp.19-20). Replication: negative binomial regression of count of threat-minimizing tweets on ideology, county COVID death rate, their interaction, county demographics, political lean and state fixed effects, following Block Jr et al. (2022) (pp.21-22).
findings: Stance is distinct from sentiment and should be measured independently; sentiment can inform intensity but does not replace stance (Section 2.1, pp.2-3).
Ambiguity is higher when the document does not mention Trump: 34.0% of non-Trump documents versus 19.5% of Trump-mentioning documents had conflicting human codes (Section 3.3, p.10).
NLI classifiers degrade most when Trump is not mentioned; supervised and in-context classifiers adapt better to low-context documents (Figure 2, p.10).

Supervised results (Table 3, p.12, Twitter only): logistic regression MCC 0.51, random forest 0.49, SVM 0.49, RoBERTa 0.60, BERTweet 0.63, PoliBERTweet 0.68 (best); DeBERTaV3 base without domain adaptation 0.63.
Laurer et al. (2024), cited on p.12: 500 training examples let language models consistently beat other algorithms trained on several thousand.
NLI results (Table 4, p.14): DeBERTaV3 Small MCC 0.15, Base 0.40, Large 0.65 (83% accuracy); only the Large model is described as comparable to supervised classifiers and human-level.

works.title: Politics of Feelings: Emotional Expression and Legislative Effectiveness in the U.S. Congress
works.summary: Aroyehun (arXiv 2609.10198, Sep 2026) scores 1,766,113 Congressional Record floor speeches (93rd-118th Congresses, 1973-2024) for eight discrete emotions with a transformer multilabel classifier (Widmann and Wich 2023), z-standardized over the corpus. Four questions: trends (Mann-Kendall over 26 Congress means: nearly every emotion rises in both parties, read as intensification rather than a negative turn), policy domains (all eight differ across 21 CAP topics, but epsilon squared only 0.013-0.034), member correlates (mixed models: majority members show less anger, -0.035; senators less anger, -0.041; women more enthusiasm, +0.020; ideology score more anger, +0.022; marginal R2 0.003-0.071), and legislative effectiveness. On the Volden-Wiseman LES (member-Congress, n = 13,671), enthusiasm (+0.016) and pride (+0.011) are positive, anger (-0.037) is the only negative, and emotional diversity (+0.026 to +0.031) and valence (+0.020) beat intensity (-0.014). Marginal R2 moves only from about 0.113 to 0.119, so emotion adds little beyond the controls. The design is associational: no identification strategy, reverse causation is not addressed, validation is 50 extreme-scored speeches per emotion in-domain only, the classifier was built on German political text, and the paper has internal inconsistencies (random intercepts vs fixed effects, table labels). For Paul's systems it matters in three places. It uses the same CEL LES that fec/members/lep_criterion.py pulls as an external criterion. It shows speech-emotion features vary with chamber, majority status and gender, which the affective-N slot controls only partly. And its valence vs intensity split matches the two LSD fields already computed in Draft Systems. Nothing here justifies adding an emotion feature to rank. All coefficients are UNVERIFIED in this project (DE-062).
works.question: RQ1: how have discrete emotions in U.S. congressional speeches evolved over time, and how do Democrats and Republicans differ? RQ2: how do discrete emotions vary across CAP policy domains? RQ3: how does legislators emotional expression vary with demographic and socio-political characteristics? RQ4: do discrete emotions and broader emotional characteristics (valence, intensity, diversity) explain variation in legislative effectiveness?
works.method: Transformer multilabel classifier (Widmann and Wich 2023) gives continuous scores for eight emotions per speech, z-standardized over the corpus (Sec 3.2.1). RQ1: Mann-Kendall with Sen slope, Benjamini-Hochberg FDR (Table 3). RQ2: CAP topic means and Kruskal-Wallis across 21 topics (Table 4). RQ3: linear mixed-effects per emotion, legislator random intercept, Congress fixed effects, topic controls (Tables 5-6). RQ4: mixed-effects models of member-Congress LES on each emotion or on valence, intensity, diversity (Tables 7-9).
findings: RQ1 trends (Sec 4.1, Table 3): Mann-Kendall finds significant increasing trends in mean emotion scores for nearly all emotions in both parties across 26 Congresses. Exception: Democratic joy (tau 0.243, FDR p 0.086). Democratic enthusiasm Sen slope 0.030 per Congress.

Parallel paths (Sec 4.1, Sec 5): Democrats and Republicans follow similar trajectories for most emotions. Authors read the rise as broad intensification of emotional expression, not a shift toward negative rhetoric, since positive and negative emotions both rise.

Anger is volatile (Sec 4.1, Fig 1): Democratic anger peaks in the early 2000s and around 2017; Republican anger is higher in 2021 to 2024. Authors link this volatility to prevailing political context.

Policy domains (RQ2, Sec 4.2, Table 4, Fig 2): Kruskal-Wallis differences significant for all eight emotions across 21 CAP topics, with small effect sizes (epsilon squared 0.013 to 0.034). International Affairs has highest mean fear; Immigration highest mean anger; Education highest pride with elevated joy and enthusiasm; Macroeconomics pairs high anger with low joy and pride.

Demographic and party correlates (RQ3, Sec 4.3, Tables 5-6): female legislators higher enthusiasm (0.020), pride (0.012), joy (0.007), sadness (0.006) and fear (0.004) in standardized units. Senators: lower anger (-0.041) and enthusiasm (-0.007), higher pride (0.009) and joy (0.008). Ideology score: higher anger (0.022), lower joy (-0.004), enthusiasm (-0.002) and pride (-0.006). Marginal R2 ranges 0.003 to 0.071.

Majority party (Tables 5-6): majority members express more joy (0.003), enthusiasm (0.006) and pride (0.009), and less anger (-0.035) and fear (-0.001). Republican coefficients are small, and Republicans express more joy (0.005) and pride (0.005) but less anger (-0.012).

works.title: Political DEBATE: Efficient Zero-shot and Few-shot Classifiers for Political Text
works.summary: Burnham, Kahn, Wang and Peng (arXiv 2024) release Political DEBATE: DeBERTa V3 base (86M) and large (304M) NLI classifiers, further trained on PolNLI. PolNLI holds 201,691 political documents and 852 hypotheses across stance, topic, hate-speech and event tasks, and its sources include congressional newsletters. On test hypotheses unseen in training, both models beat general NLI models, Llama 3.1 8B and Claude 3.5 Sonnet on zero-shot MCC. On the hardest stance set (quote tweets), Claude scores MCC 0.29, base 0.62 and large 0.88. In few-shot training, 10 to 25 random labeled documents are often enough. The base model, however, failed the bespoke COVID threat-minimization task and could not match a supervised classifier (MCC 0.66) even at 100 samples, while the large model matched it at 10 (0.67). The authors therefore recommend the large model whenever feasible, short single-condition hypotheses, and supervised training when labels need meta-knowledge or a bespoke concept. The labels were validated with GPT-4o, so GPT-4o is excluded from the benchmark. For Paul, this is the actual checkpoint behind the Melange CU press stance reader. The system fine-tunes the base model on 552 labeled releases. Its own history follows the paper's pattern: base zero-shot reached 53% accuracy with oppose F1 0.08, and fine-tuning raised it to 87% agreement with Claude. Its valence-hop bottleneck matches the paper's warning about bespoke concepts. The bearings are on the model choice (base, not large), hypothesis design (a compound neutral hypothesis), the evaluation metric (accuracy and kappa against an LLM reference rather than MCC against humans), and the planned ACU speaker-mode branching. Nothing here touches the SNA or LDA rules.
works.question: Can small, domain-adapted natural language inference (NLI) encoder models trained on political text match or beat zero-shot large language models and supervised classifiers for political text classification, and can they be few-shot trained from 10-25 labeled documents, while staying open and efficient? (p.1-2)
works.method: Fine-tunes DeBERTa V3 base (86M parameters) and large (304M) models that were already trained for general NLI (Laurer et al. 2023), using the Transformers library (p.2, p.8). Label cleaning removes source metadata; hypotheses are written per label (p.5-6). Labels are validated by GPT-4o; documents where human and LLM labels disagree are dropped (p.6-7). Hypotheses are augmented with GPT-4o synonyms and manual review (p.7). Checkpoints chosen by training loss, validation loss, MCC, F1, accuracy and per-task consistency, plus qualitative tests with punctuation, capitalization and wording edits (p.8). Zero-shot benchmark against DeBERTa base and large NLI (Laurer et al. 2023), Llama 3.1 8B and Claude 3.5 Sonnet; GPT-4o not benchmarked (p.9). Few-shot: simple random samples of 10, 25, 50 and 100 documents, 10 repetitions each, 95% confidence intervals, default learning rate, 5 epochs, no hyperparameter or hypothesis search (p.12). Timing: same 5,000 documents with hypothesis 'This text is about politics' on RTX 3090, Tesla T4, M3 Max and Ryzen 9 5900x (p.14).
findings: PolNLI test set, all tasks combined: DEBATE models are more performative than DeBERTa base and large NLI, Llama 3.1 8B and Claude 3.5 Sonnet in zero-shot MCC; per-model values appear only in Fig. 1 (p.9-10).
Stance: DEBATE models and Claude 3.5 Sonnet are significantly better than the other models on stance detection; event extraction is comparable between DEBATE and the two LLMs (p.9).
Hate-speech: DEBATE models are significantly better than the other models; the authors attribute this to subjective definitions that the models were tuned to (p.9-10).
Polistance Quote Tweets (stance, hardest set): Claude 3.5 MCC 0.29; DEBATE base MCC 0.62 and large MCC 0.88; DeBERTa Large had negative correlation with the correct label on this dataset (p.10).

Few-shot, Mood of the Nation liberty and rights: Llama 3.1 is best zero-shot (reported MCC 0.74, accuracy 88%); after 10 samples both DEBATE models jump and do not differ significantly from Llama; at 25 the large model significantly beats Llama; at 50 the base model matches it (p.13).

Few-shot, COVID-19 threat minimization: base model largely fails zero-shot and does not match the supervised Electra classifier (MCC 0.66 on 2,000 tweets) at 100 samples; large model matches it at 10 samples (MCC 0.67, accuracy 87%) and exceeds it at 25 (MCC 0.69, accuracy 88%) (p.13-14).

related.why: Same first author. The paper defers to Burnham (2024), Stance detection: a practical guide in Political Science Research and Methods, for NLI best practice and cites its finding that larger NLI models generalize better to unseen tasks. The item is dated 2023 (arXiv 2305.01723, PSRM 2025); the paper cites 2024.

Compares fine-tuned RoBERTa with traditional ML for political-tweet stance, the transformer-versus-SVM question the system's supervised stack and DEBATE reader raise. The paper itself does not cite it.

Paul's vault cites it as the anchor for LLM position labels (GPT-4 zero-shot, 96.9 percent on keyword-prefiltered lobbying lines). DEBATE is the small open NLI alternative the system runs. Kim's task does not transfer directly.

Paul's vault cites its personality-cue result: few-shot LLM prompting 0.77 beats fine-tuned XLM-RoBERTa 0.70, which beats a bag-of-words SVM 0.63. The cited line does not name GPT-4o. DEBATE is a small NLI encoder in a different slot.

Paul's vault describes it as fusing three LLM decisions by attention routing for stance on VAST, not an NLI method. It is a possible comparator for the NLI reader, not the same method.

works.title: Large language models know how the personality of public figures is perceived by the general public
works.summary: Cao and Kosinski (Scientific Reports 14:6735, 2024) fit ridge regressions from 12,288-dimensional GPT-3 embeddings of public figures' NAMES to mean human ratings of perceived Big Five traits and likability (N = 226 Pantheon figures from 43 countries, 600 Prolific raters, about 19 ratings per figure, TIPI items). With 20-fold cross-validation, predictions correlate with aggregate perceptions at r = .78 to .88 after attenuation correction (raw .70 to .80). Controlling for likability and demographics (birth year, gender), accuracy falls to corrected r = .53 to .70 (raw .43 to .61). Accuracy rises with popularity (r = .16 with log Wikipedia views). The design is predictive, not causal, and concerns PERCEIVED, not actual, personality. For Melange the paper is the cited motivation for de-identifying text before the Pink LLM trait reader: a model that knows a politician's name carries a reputational prior that can stand in for reading the text. The paper shows the prior exists for famous names; it does not test whether stripping names, titles, party and states from congressional text removes it, and the repo's --named contamination probe has no output artifact in data/members. The likability result bears on the halo questions: a large evaluative factor runs through perceptions of public figures, yet trait-specific signal survives its removal, consistent with the CT-CM design of one halo method factor plus traits, and a caution that perception-based gold panels are not halo-free criteria. The code cites the work as PNAS Nexus 2024 with r = .76 to .87; the vault copy is Scientific Reports with corrected r = .78 to .88, so that citation needs checking.
works.question: Can the perceived personality of public figures (Big Five traits and likability) be predicted from the location of their names in GPT-3's semantic embedding space, and does this hold after controlling for likability and demographics?
works.method: Ridge regression of mean human ratings on column-standardized GPT-3 name embeddings, with 20-fold cross-validation (each figure predicted by a model trained on all others) and alpha tuned in an inner 20-fold loop. Controlled models first regress each trait on likability plus demographics (birth year, gender) and then predict the residuals from embeddings. Correlations are corrected for attenuation by dividing by the square root of split-half reliability (0.79-0.88). Effect sizes converted to Cohen's d. Interpretation by projecting 525 person-descriptive adjectives onto the fitted regression lines.
findings: Without controls, cross-validated predictions correlate with human ratings r = 0.78 (extraversion) to 0.88 (openness) after attenuation correction; raw r 0.70-0.80. Results p.2 and Figure 1 green bars.
Translated to Cohen's d, the no-controls correlations give d = 2.49 to 3.75 (labelled huge effects). Results p.2.

Controlling for likability and demographics, accuracy falls to r = 0.53 (emotional stability) to 0.70 (extraversion) after correction; raw r 0.43-0.61 (d = 1.25-1.96). Results p.4 and Figure 1 red bars.

Benchmarks used by authors: no-controls accuracy compared with CT detection of head and neck metastases (r = 0.64) and ultrasound for peripheral artery disease (r = 0.83); controlled accuracy compared with dental X-ray cavity detection (r = 0.43) and ultrasound for deep venous thrombosis (r = 0.60). Results p.3-4.
Self-reported Big Five from language is cited as about r = 0.40 for comparison. Results p.4.
Embeddings predict aggregate human judgments better than individual judgments do: single-rater to aggregate correlation r = 0.56-0.66. Results p.3.

Meta-analysis of Big Five prediction from digital footprints. Cao's about r = .40 language benchmark is cited to Park et al. 2015 (ref 39), not to this meta-analysis, so the same-method label is not supported.

Review of personality computing that lists data privacy among its threats. Cao's privacy framing (Discussion p.6) rests on Kosinski's work instead, so the two are complementary rather than sources for each other.

works.title: Impressive Words: Linguistic Predictors of Public Approval of the U.S. Congress
works.summary: Decter-Frain and Frimer (Frontiers in Psychology 2016) ask whether the language spoken on the House floor tracks public approval of Congress. They built a monthly series from January 1996 to November 2014 (N = 206 months, about 124 million words) and scored it with LIWC 2007. Agency and communion indexes come from five coders who weighted each category (ICC 0.82 and 0.90). A separate 127-word prosocial (helping) dictionary is scored alongside them. The outcome is monthly Gallup approval. Both broad indexes correlate negatively with approval: agency r = -0.16 and communion r = -0.36. With controls, agency stays negative (beta -0.11) and communion is null. Prosocial language correlates r = +0.55 and survives the controls (beta +0.14). Media tone partly mediates all three. An exploratory stepwise pass keeps 8 of 63 categories, and the authors call these only suggestive. Moderation by the gender and party make-up of the chamber flips some signs. The design is correlational, aggregate and chamber-level, and the authors rule out causal claims. For Paul's systems the sharpest point is about construct definition. Communion is not one thing. The helping facet and the broader communion or belonging facet behave in opposite directions against an audience-perception outcome. Melange's persona channel uses one communion share from an LLM cue codebook (empathy and compassion), and that share feeds receptivity at PERSONA_W 0.30. That codebook already sits close to the helping facet, which is reassuring. But the paper's outcome is public approval of the institution, not a member's openness to lobbying, so it neither validates nor undercuts the susceptibility mapping. It also offers a cheap dictionary-based second path for checking the LLM cue shares.
works.question: Which demeanor makes the best impression in a professional setting: agentic (competent) language, communal (warm) language, or a specific linguistic category? Tested by predicting monthly public approval of the U.S. Congress from the words used in House floor debates, first theory-driven, then exploratory.
works.method: Word density per LIWC 2007 category (63) plus a 127-word prosocial dictionary. Five blind coders scored each category +1, 0 or -1 for agency and communion (ICC communion 0.90, agency 0.82). Indexes = z-scored densities times weights, summed. Pearson correlations; OLS Models 1 to 3 (Model 3 adds controls); z tests comparing correlations; Hayes bootstrapped mediation via media tone; exploratory stepwise regression over 63 categories (entry p < 0.005, removal p > 0.01).
findings: Simple correlations with approval are negative for both agency (r = -0.16, p < 0.05) and communion (r = -0.36, p < 0.001). Hypothesis 1 not supported. Table 2, p.7.
With all controls (Model 3), agency is a significant negative predictor (beta -0.11, p < 0.05) and communion is not (beta +0.04). Table 2, p.7.
Prosocial language correlates r = +0.55 (p < 0.001) with approval and stays a positive predictor with controls (beta +0.14, p < 0.05). Table 3, p.8. Supports Hypothesis 2.

Prosocial and agency correlations differ significantly (z = 7.89, p < 0.001); communion and agency also differ (z = 2.18, p = 0.03), but both are negative. The authors read this as support for Hypothesis 3b. Results, p.8.
Media tone carries indirect effects: agency B = -0.11 [-0.30, -0.02], communion -0.06 [-0.16, -0.01], prosocial +1.82 [0.17, 5.26]. Direct effects of all three are also significant. Table 4, p.8.

Moderation (text only; numbers are in the Supplement): agency predicts disapproval only when Congress is male-dominated; communal language is approved when Congress is male-dominated and disapproved otherwise; prosocial effect is stronger with fewer men and more Republicans. Results, p.8. The authors call these results mixed.

related.why: Same agency and communion constructs for politicians. Birkenmaier and Lechner use LLM cue prompting, the instrument Melange runs; this paper uses coder-weighted LIWC dictionaries. Together they give two measurement paths.

Both score Congressional Record House floor speech over 1996 to 2014 with closed-vocabulary categories. Ramey does it at member level for traits, and this paper does it at chamber-month level for approval. Verified in the Ramey item.
LIWC word-category densities as psychological indicators are the measurement basis of this paper.
Meta-analysis of how far LIWC categories carry Big Five signal. It bounds how much the coder-weighted LIWC agency and communion indexes can mean.

The PoliPers framework for politicians' agency and communion profiles is the source of the codebook Melange uses, per the agency_communion_llm.py docstring. This paper adds the belonging versus helping split.
Also treats parliamentary rhetoric as aimed at an outside audience, but works on emotive language where this paper works on agentic and communal language.
Emotional expression in congressional speech linked to legislative effectiveness at member level; this paper links language to chamber-level approval.
Politician personality and media visibility relate to this paper's finding that media tone mediates the language-approval link.

works.title: No Longer Conforming to Stereotypes? Gender, Political Style, and Parliamentary Debate in the UK
works.summary: Hargrave and Blumenau (UCL working paper; the text is dated October 2021, filed here as 2022) track how gendered debating style changed in the UK House of Commons between May 1997 and March 2019. The corpus is 418,147 MP-debate observations: 1,422 MPs across 14,864 debates. They score eight styles. Three are communal: human narrative, affect and positive emotion. Five are agentic: fact, complexity, repetition, aggression and negative emotion. Six of the measures come from seed dictionaries expanded with GloVe embeddings, and these beat standard dictionaries against human coding for every style except fact (positive emotion about 0.70 against 0.38). Each style goes through a Bayesian dynamic hierarchical model with debate random effects, so gender gaps are estimated within debates. Early in the period, women used more communal styles and men more aggression and complexity. Women also used more fact, repetition and negative emotion, which runs against the stereotype. For six of eight styles the share of between-MP variation explained by gender fell, by 29 to 60 percent comparing the periods before and after 2007. Fact and negative emotion went the other way, rising to about 4 and 9 percent of MP-level variation after 2007. The change sits mostly with women, whose communal styles declined. The work is observational and does not separate mechanisms. For Paul's systems, the main point is that agency, communion and negative-emotion text scores can carry a gender signature that changes over time. The persona channel and affective N in the receptivity layer check for a party signature but not for gender. This is UK floor debate measured with dictionaries, not the US Congress, so any transfer is a hypothesis to test, not a finding.
works.question: Have gender gaps in parliamentary debating style, measured against gender stereotypes, narrowed in the UK House of Commons since 1997, and are women moving toward agentic styles over time (p.2-3, p.12)?
works.method: Eight style measures from text. Six use word-embedding expanded seed dictionaries (GloVe, 150 dimensions, window 3; sigmoid rescaling a=40, c=0.35; TF-IDF weighted sentence scores) (p.15-17, S2-S7). Complexity uses rescaled Flesch-Kincaid. Repetition uses Lempel-Ziv compression ratio. Measures standardised to mean 0, SD 1. Outcome model: Bayesian dynamic hierarchical normal model in Stan, one fit per style (three chains, 500 iterations after 250 burn-in); MP-by-session intercepts, debate random effects, random-walk priors on male baseline and female gap across sessions (p.19-22).
findings: Early period: female MPs use more human narrative, affect and positive emotion, while men use more aggression and complexity, at least before 2010 (p.23-24).
Fact, repetition and negative emotion run against stereotype: women use them more than men for much of the period (p.23-24).
Six of eight styles: MP gender explains less between-MP variation in style at the end of the period than at the start (p.4).
For styles that converge, the share of MP-level variation explained by gender falls by between 29% and 60% comparing periods before and after 2007 (p.25).
Fact and negative emotion diverge: gender explains about 0.6% and 2% of variation in 1997-2007, rising to about 4% and 9% after 2007 (p.25).
Aggression, complexity, affect and positive emotion gaps shrink to no consistent difference in recent years; the repetition gap stays relatively stable (p.23-26).

works.title: Positioning Political Texts with Large Language Models by Asking and Averaging
works.summary: Le Mens and Gallego (arXiv 2311.16639, v3 dated September 2024) test a simple measurement recipe: ask an instruction-tuned LLM for a 0 to 100 position score for each short text (a tweet or one manifesto sentence), let it answer NA when the text is not on the dimension, and average the answered scores to place longer documents or actors. Across four settings the best models track human benchmarks closely. On 899 Congress tweets, GPT-4o reaches r=0.92 with a mean of about 20 crowd raters. For 117th-Congress senators, the comparison is with the first Nokken-Poole roll-call dimension, and r=0.97. On 18 UK manifestos, r=0.98 on the economic dimension and 0.94 on the social one, against expert coding. On 36 European Parliament coal-subsidy speeches in 10 languages, r=0.93 with crowd coding. Fine-tuned BERT, tf-idf and GloVe classifiers score lower. The headline figures are mostly between-party, though. Within-party correlations fall to 0.66 to 0.72 for tweets and senators. On the pro/anti-subsidy dimension, the Against group drops to 0.04 to 0.07 for every model except GPT-4o. All validity evidence is concurrent correlation, and Claude models were not tested. For Paul's systems, the paper supports using an LLM as a stance rater and contrasts with classical TF-IDF readers. It also points to three things the CU stance pipeline does not yet have: a continuous position score, explicit not-applicable handling kept separate from neutral, and validity reported within party. Because the paper's dimensions are left-right and pro/anti-subsidy, it cannot validate the target-specific credit-union stance on its own.
works.question: Can instruction-tuned LLMs position short texts (tweets, sentences) on ideological or policy dimensions by directly asking for a 0 to 100 score and averaging those scores to position longer texts and political actors, and how do the estimates compare with expert, crowd, roll-call, campaign-finance and classifier benchmarks?
works.method: Direct query: LLM gives a 0 to 100 JSON Score on a left-right, economic, social or pro/anti-subsidy scale, NA allowed for non-political text; temperature 0, max 20 tokens. Manifestos and speeches scored sentence by sentence and averaged. Comparators: fine-tuned BERT, GloVe and tf-idf classifiers. Validity by Pearson r with benchmarks; split-half reliability with Spearman-Brown. Robustness: dimension prompts, whole-document prompts, typicality scoring, ENO. No inference beyond correlations.
findings: Tweets (N=899, Sec 3.1, Fig 1): GPT-4o r=0.92 with crowd mean (557 scored tweets); GPT-4 r=0.90; MiXtral 8X22B 0.90; Llama 3 70Bq4 0.88; Llama 3 8B 0.80; fine-tuned BERT 0.78; tf-idf 0.66; GloVe 0.63.
Tweets within party (Fig 1): GPT-4o r=0.68 among Democratic tweets and 0.66 among Republican tweets. Text says no classifier matches the best LLMs, especially for within-party differences.

Senators of the 117th Congress (Sec 3.2, Fig 2): GPT-4o r=0.97 with first-dimension DW-NOMINATE; GPT-4 0.97; Llama 3 70Bq4 0.97; MiXtral 8X22B 0.96; Llama 3 8B 0.96; BERT 0.93; tf-idf 0.90; GloVe 0.86. Within-party GPT-4o r=0.72 (Democrats) and 0.72 (Republicans).
Senators and CFscore (App A8, figure-only): LLM positions correlate highly with 2020 campaign-finance scores overall but less so within party; coefficients are not stated in the text.

works.title: Playing to the Gallery: Emotive Rhetoric in Parliaments
works.summary: Osnabrugge, Hobolt and Rodon (APSR 2021) ask whether legislators use emotive language strategically, raising it when a debate reaches voters rather than only colleagues. They score 958,925 UK House of Commons speeches (2001-2019) and 945,734 Irish Dail speeches (2002-2013) with a dictionary built from ANEW seed words (emotive = clearly positive or negative, neutral = neither) expanded through corpus-trained skip-gram embeddings; each speech gets percent emotive minus percent neutral words (mean 0.88, SD 8.95 on a -100 to 100 scale). OLS with MP-clustered errors shows Prime Minister's Questions speeches score 2.23 points higher than ordinary debates, and 1.56 to 1.66 higher within the same MP once MP fixed effects are added; the Queen's Speech opening day is similar, Ministerial Question Time is slightly lower, and topic fixed effects do not remove the gap. Ireland's Leaders' Questions shows 2.5 to 4.6. The electoral-cycle effect is tiny (0.015 per 100 days). The authors state the design is observational and cannot causally identify audience exposure. For Paul's systems the paper matters in two places. First, it is direct evidence that the same speaker's affect-word rates move with venue and audience, which bears on the lexical Big Five and affective-N slots: Melange pools social posts, floor speech and interviews per member before z-scoring, and the interview-to-floor N transfer already failed. It supports Paul's ask for venue-specific frameworks. Second, its valence-agnostic emotive score is closer to the unused lsd_charge option than to the live abs(net)/words intensity in the press pipeline, and its audience logic cautions that press-release heat may index performance for the public rather than commitment.
works.question: When and why do legislators use emotive rhetoric in parliamentary speeches? Is emotive language used strategically to appeal to voters, so that it rises when a debate has a larger public audience?
works.method: Dictionary score per speech = percent emotive words minus percent neutral words, -100 to 100 (p. 6-7). Dictionary: ANEW seeds (851 emotive, 970 neutral) expanded with skip-gram embeddings (window 10, 250 dims) and cosine scoring against seeds; final 2,015 emotive and 2,095 neutral words (UK), 1,692 and 1,764 (Ireland). OLS, SEs clustered by MP, five specifications (baseline, time trend, MP fixed effects, controls and party FE, length-weighted MP FE). Topic check: scikit-learn classifier trained on Manifesto corpus, seven topics, used as topic fixed effects (Table 4).
findings: Baseline model (Table 3, Model 1, p. 8): speeches in PMQs score 2.226 points higher on the emotive-minus-neutral scale (SE 0.128, p<0.01).
With time trend, MP fixed effects and controls (Model 4, p. 8-9): PMQs effect 1.618 (SE 0.167); MP fixed effects alone (Model 3) 1.562 (SE 0.137).
Length-weighted MP fixed-effects model (Model 5, p. 9): PMQs 1.663 (SE 0.214) and Queen's Speech opening day 2.064 (SE 0.166).
Queen's Speech opening day debate: 2.172 in Model 1 (SE 0.214); other Queen's Speech days 0.581 (SE 0.106), p. 8.
Ministerial Question Time is slightly negative (-0.293 in Model 1; -0.207 in Model 5); Urgent Questions effect not robust (Table 3, p. 8-9).
Predicted levels from Model 4 (Figure 3, p. 9): about 2.5 for PMQs, about 3.0 for Queen's Speech opening day, 1.5 for other Queen's Speech days, and 1.0 or lower for other debate types.

works.title: Large Language Models Can Infer Psychological Dispositions of Social Media Users
works.summary: Peters and Matz test whether off-the-shelf chat models can read Big Five personality from ordinary social media text with no training. They took 1,000 MyPersonality Facebook users (2007-2012, mean age 24, 63 percent women) who had completed the 100-item IPIP and had at least 200 status updates. GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 (2023 snapshots) were asked zero-shot for a 1-5 score on each trait. Text went in 20-message chunks, chunk scores were averaged, and each call was repeated three times and averaged. Inferred scores correlate with self-report at a mean r of .29: .31 for GPT-4 and .27 for GPT-3.5, with a per-trait range of .22-.33. Supervised in-domain models reach about .37. Accuracy is mostly reached by about 20 messages. Both models shift levels: they underestimate Conscientiousness and Agreeableness and overestimate Neuroticism. Absolute errors are larger for men on C, A and N, and for older users under GPT-3.5. Within-group correlations do not differ, so the bias is in level, not rank order. In a subsample of 68 users rated by friends, LLM-observer agreement (about .27) is close to self-observer agreement (.30). For Conscientiousness the LLM agrees more with observers than with self-report. For Melange, the paper backs the design of the display-only LLM item reader (chunk, then average) and sets a realistic ceiling for zero-shot accuracy. It also warns that agreement with observer panels may reflect shared impressions rather than traits. And it gives a reason to check the live affective-N input, which is partly LLM-derived, for gender as well as party bias. The population, text genre and criterion are all far from congressional speech, so none of its numbers can stand in as validity evidence for Melange.
works.question: Can zero-shot GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 infer the Big Five personality traits of social media users from their Facebook status updates, and does inference accuracy vary across gender and age groups?
works.method: Zero-shot prompting with default system prompt 'You are a helpful assistant' and an inference prompt asking for 1-5 scores on each Big Five trait, numbers only (Sec 2.2). Text fed in chunks of 20 messages; chunk scores averaged. Each inference queried three times and averaged (inter-round r from .73 to .96). Analyses: Pearson correlations between inferred and self-reported scores with Bonferroni correction; mean comparisons across gender and a median-split age groups by t-tests on inferred scores and on absolute residuals; within-group correlations and within-group z-standardization to test whether bias is in level versus rank order (Sec 3.2); correlations by message volume from 20 to 200 messages (Sec 3.1); observer-rating comparison (Sec 3.3).
findings: Average Pearson r between inferred and self-reported traits: GPT-3.5 .27, GPT-4 .31 (Sec 3.1). Abstract reports average .29, range .22-.33 across both models.

GPT-4 per-trait r: Openness .33, Extraversion .32, Agreeableness .32, Neuroticism .29, Conscientiousness .26. GPT-3.5: Openness .28, Extraversion .29, Agreeableness .30, Neuroticism .26, Conscientiousness .22 (Sec 3.1).
All correlations significant at p below .001 after Bonferroni correction. Differences between GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 not significant for any single trait (Sec 3.1).
Accuracy rises with message volume; most of the maximum is reached by about 20 messages. Conscientiousness levels off earlier (Sec 3.1, Fig 2).

Score distributions: both models underestimate Conscientiousness and Agreeableness and overestimate Neuroticism. GPT-3.5 underestimates Openness and Extraversion; GPT-4 overestimates Extraversion (Sec 3.1, Fig 1).

Gender: inferred Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion and Agreeableness are higher for women in both models (Agreeableness t=13.63 for GPT-4). No significant inferred Neuroticism difference (Sec 3.2.1, Fig 3).

related.why: Cao and Kosinski show that LLM-derived perceptions of public figures can be predicted from name embeddings alone (text check of the paper). That is the reputational-prior risk the de-identification step guards against, and it bears on how observer agreement is read.
The note confirms Azucar, Marengo and Settanni as the meta-analysis Peters cites as ref 15. Published 2018 (online Dec 2017); the slug year is 2017, a naming difference only.
The note reports few-shot prompting of DeepSeek-V3 and GPT-4o reaching macro-F1 0.74-0.77 on elite text for agency and communion cues. This is the elite-text genre Peters does not cover.
Meta-analysis of Big Five and LIWC relations, the closed-vocabulary baseline against which zero-shot LLM inference is compared. Published 2022; the slug year is 2024, a naming difference only.
The appendix gives the Senate insider and academic observer panels used as the system criterion. Its text-count of academic rows (about 126) differs from the 125 in the gold-set note.
Title and text confirm a design of asking an LLM about each text and averaging the responses, parallel to Peters' three-query averaging.

Ramey et al. run floor speech through LIWC and MRC features with pre-trained Mairesse SMOreg models, a closed-vocabulary approach on elite speech. Peters is the open-ended LLM alternative on non-elite text.

Palm and Tims is a systematic review of whether Big Five traits moderate persuasion strategies. The research note lists its evidence status as unverified, so this link is kept on the note's abstract only.

works.title: Measuring Emotion in Parliamentary Debates with Automated Textual Analysis
works.summary: Rheault, Beelen, Cochrane and Hirst build a domain-adapted emotion lexicon for the UK House of Commons (Hansard 1909-2013, about 957 million tokens). They train 300-dimension GloVe vectors on lemma-PoS pairs, score each word by cosine similarity to 100 positive minus 100 negative emotion seeds, and keep the 4,200 most polar words. Period polarity is the lexicon-weighted sum divided by all lemmas, with a negation window to punctuation. Debate grows more positive over the century, and the rise holds under NRC, OpinionFinder and SentiWordNet. Recession years lower annual polarity change (ARMAX -0.198, SE 0.062, N=104 years, pooled over government and opposition, so UNSTRATIFIED). Election years raise it (+0.187). Labor disputes Granger-cause polarity (chi2 9.42, p=.002) but not the reverse. Split by side, the effect runs through the opposition (chi2 8.05, p=.005) and not the government (p=.761). The design is associational, and the authors say the cointegrating relation is not causal. The lexicon is validated only on film reviews, never on parliamentary speech. For Paul's systems the work matters in three places. It is the method source for the opt-in GloVe seed-expansion helper in the legacy press scorer. It qualifies the general-purpose LSD2015 tone intensity that feeds press_value: domain adaptation is argued for, the default intensity is |net|/words (a polarity magnitude, not a charge), and macro-period shifts in tone are not removed. And it shows that negative-emotion language in a legislature follows institutional role (opposition vs government) and economic shocks. That bears on the affective-N slot, which controls for party but not for majority status or period. All three are UNVERIFIED single-agent readings (DE-062).
works.question: Can domain-adapted affective text analysis measure the emotional polarity of UK parliamentary debates over a century, and does that polarity change over time and respond to national economic conditions such as recessions and labor disputes?
works.method: Word vectors: GloVe, 300 dimensions per lemma-PoS pair, symmetric window of 15 tokens (p.3). Seeds: 200 hand-picked English emotion lemmas, 100 positive and 100 negative (p.3). Lexicon: each lemma scored in [-1,1] by summed cosine similarity to positive minus negative seeds (Eq 1, p.4); top and bottom 2000 kept, giving 4200 words. Polarity y_t: lexicon-weighted mean score divided by the count of all lemmas in the period, with a negation flag zeroing words between a negation cue and punctuation (Eqs 2-3, p.5). Stationarity: Dickey-Fuller and KPSS tests, unit root found (pp.8, S1 Appendix Tables A-D). Main model: ARMAX on first differences with recession and election dummies and 1 or 2 lags, maximum likelihood (Eq 5, Table 2, p.9). Group tests: one-sided t-tests on mean differences (Table 3, p.10). Granger causality: pairwise augmented VAR chi-square tests (Table 4, p.13). Cointegration: Johansen rank test; bivariate VECM with 2 lags in levels, orthogonalized impulse response with bootstrap bands (Fig 4, pp.12-13). Long-run effect: dynamic OLS with HAC standard errors (p.12). Long memory: spectral regression of log power on frequency, alpha in 1/f^alpha (p.7).
findings: Polarity rises over 1909-2013: debates become more positive in recent decades (Fig 1, p.6; text pp.5-7). The rise is robust to NRC, OpinionFinder and SentiWordNet lexicons (S1 Fig, p.7) and appears in government and opposition series (Fig 2, p.8). No slope coefficient is reported in the text.

Recession years lower the annual change in polarity: coefficient -0.198 (SE 0.062) in ARMAX Model 1 and -0.165 (SE 0.063) in Model 2, both significant at 95 percent. Autoregressive terms rho1 -0.275 (SE 0.095) and -0.313 (SE 0.098); rho2 -0.145 (SE 0.104). N=104 years (Table 2, p.9).
Election years raise polarity: coefficient 0.187 (SE 0.069) and 0.183 (SE 0.069) in the two ARMAX models (Table 2, p.9). Text says a similar order of magnitude, about 0.19.

Mean-difference t-tests (Table 3, p.10): recession years differ from other years by -0.219 (t=-2.895, p=0.002; 21 recession years against 83 others). Election years differ by 0.202 (t=2.735, p=0.004). War years differ by 0.002 (p=0.511, not significant).

Granger causality (Table 4, p.13): labor disputes Granger-cause polarity (chi2 9.424, df 1, p=0.002) but polarity does not Granger-cause labor disputes (chi2 0.056, p=0.813). Unemployment, misery index and GDP growth show no significant Granger effect in either direction (all p at least 0.12).

Cointegration (Johansen test, S1 Appendix Table F, p.12): fitted long-run relation y_t = -0.06 - 1.39 x_t (Eq 6, p.12), with x_t the labor disputes indicator. The series stay negatively related, more than one standard deviation apart; authors say this is not a causal effect.
